pacific.etymology: L. pacificus: cf. F. pacifique. See Pacify.

pacification.etymology: L. pacificatio: cf. F. pacification. See Pacify.

pacify.etymology: F. pacifier, L. pacificare; pax, pacis, peace + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Peace, and -fy.

pack.etymology: Akin to D. pakken, G. packen, Dan. pakke, Sw. packa, Icel. pakka. See Pack, n.

packet.etymology: F. paquet, dim. fr. LL. paccus, from the same source as E. pack. See Pack.

pact.etymology: L. pactum, fr. paciscere to make a bargain or contract, fr. pacere to settle, or agree upon; cf. pangere to fasten, Gr. paca bond, and E. fang: cf. F. pacie. Cf. Peace, Fadge, v.

pad.etymology: D. pad. sq. root21. See Path.

paddock.etymology: OE. padde toad, frog + -ock; akin to D. pad, padde, toad, Icel. & Sw. padda, Dan. padde.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to form diminutives; as, bullock, hillock.

padlock.etymology: Perh. orig., a lock for a pad gate, or a gate opening to a path, or perh., a lock for a basket or pannier, and from Prov. E. pad a pannier. Cf. Pad a path, Paddler.

pagan.etymology: L. paganus a countryman, peasant, villager, a pagan, fr. paganus of or pertaining to the country, rustic, also, pagan, fr. pagus a district, canton, the country, perh. orig., a district with fixed boundaries: cf. pangere to fasten. Cf. Painim, Peasant, and Pact, also Heathen.

paganism.etymology: L. paganismus: cf. F. paganisme. See Pagan, and cf. Painim.

page.etymology: F., fr. It. paggio, LL. pagius, fr. Gr. puer. Cf. Pedagogue, Puerile.

pageant.etymology: OE. pagent, pagen, originally, a movable scaffold or stage, hence, what was exhibited on it, fr. LL. pagina, akin to pangere to fasten; cf. L. pagina page, leaf, slab, compaginare to join together, compages a joining together, structure. See Pact, Page of a book.

pagoda.etymology: Pg. pagoda, pagode, fr.Hind. & Per. but-kadah a house of idols, or abode of God; Per. but an idol + kadah a house, a temple.

pail.etymology: OE. paile, AS. pægel a wine vessel, a pail, akin to D. & G. pegel a watermark, a gauge rod, a measure of wine, Dan. pægel half a pint.

paillasse.etymology: F., fr. paille straw. See Pallet a bed.

pain.etymology: OE. peine, F. peine, fr. L. poena, penalty, punishment, torment, pain; akin to Gr. penalty. Cf. Penal, Pine to languish, Punish.

paint.etymology: OE. peinten, fr. F. peint, p. p. opeindre to paint, fr. L. pingere, pictum; cf. Gr. many-colored, Skr. pic to adorn. Cf. Depict, Picture, Pigment, Pint.

painter.etymology: OE, pantere a noose, snare, F. pantière, LL. panthera, L. panther a hunting net, fr. Gr. ; painteir a net, gin, snare, Gael. painntear.

pair.etymology: F. paire, LL. paria, L. paria, pl. of par pair, fr. par, adj., equal. Cf. Apparel, Par equality, Peer an equal.

palace.etymology: OE. palais, F. palais, fr. L. palatium, fr. Palatium, one of the seven hills of Rome, Paladin.

paladin.etymology: F., fr.It. paladino, fr. L. palatinus an officer of the palace. See Palatine.

palanquin.etymology: F. palanquin, Pg. palanquim, Javan. palangki, OJavan. palangkan, through Prakrit fr. Skr. parya, palya, bed, couch; pari around (akin to E. pref. peri-) + a a hook, flank, probably akin to E. angle fishing tackle. Cf. Palkee.

roots.meaning: A prefix used to signify around, by, near, over, beyond, or to give an intensive sense; as, perimeter, the measure around; perigee, point near the earth; periergy, work beyond what is needed; perispherical, quite spherical.

palate.etymology: L. palatum: cf. F. palais, Of. also palat.

palatine.etymology: F. palatin, L. palatinus, fr. palatium. See Palace, and cf. Paladin.

palaver.etymology: Sp. palabra, or Pg. palavra, fr. L. parabola a comparison, a parable, LL., a word. See Parable.

pale.etymology: F. pâle, fr. pâlir to turn pale, L. pallere to be oAppall, Fallow, pall, v. i., Pallid.

pali.etymology: Ceylonese, fr. Skr. pali row, line, series, applied to the series of Buddhist sacred texts.

palinurus.etymology: So called from L. Palinurus, the pilot of Æneas.

palisade.etymology: F. palissade, cf. Sp. palizada, It. palizzata, palizzo, LL. palissata; all fr. L. palus a stake, pale. See Pale a stake.

pall.etymology: OE. pal, AS. pæl, from L. pallium cover, cloak, mantle, pall; cf. L. palla robe, mantle.

pallet.etymology: OE. paillet, F. paillet a heap of straw, fr. paille straw, fr. L. palea chaff; cf. Gr. pala straw, palava chaff. Cf. Paillasse.

palliate.etymology: L. palliatus, fr. pallium a cloak. See Pall the garment.

pallid.etymology: L. pallidus, fr. pallere to be or look pale. See pale, a.

pallone.etymology: It., a large ball, fr. palla ball. See Balloon.

pallor.etymology: L., fr. pallere to be or look pale. See Pale, a.

palm.etymology: OE. paume, F. paume, L. palma, Gr. pani hand, and E. fumble. See Fumble, Feel, and cf. 2d Palm.

palmar.etymology: L. palmaris, fr. palma the palm of the hand: cf. F. palmaire.

palmate.etymology: L. palmatus marked with the palm of a hand, from palma the palm of the hand.

palmatifid.etymology: L. palmatus palmate + root of findere to split.

palmetto.etymology: Dim. of palm the tree: cf. Sp. palmito.

palmitin.etymology: So called because abundant in palm oil.

palpable.etymology: F. palpable, L. palpabilis, fr. palpare to feel, stroke; cf. palpus the soft palm of the hand.

palpation.etymology: L. palpatio, fr. palpare. See Palpable.

palpitate.etymology: L. palpitare, palpitatum, v. intens. fr. pappare. See Palpable.

palsgrave.etymology: D. paltsgraaf; palts palace (l. palatium) + graaf count; cf. G. pfalzgraf. See Palace, and Landgrave.

palsy.etymology: OE. palesie, parlesy, OF. paralesie, F. paralysie, L. paralysis. See Paralysis.

paltry.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. paltry refuse, rubbish, LG. paltering ragged, palte, palter, a rag, a tatter, Dan. pialt, Sw. palta, pl. paltor.

pampas.etymology: Sp., fr. Peruv. pampa a field, plain.

pamper.etymology: Cf. LG. pampen, slampampen, to live luxuriously, pampe thick pap, and E. pap.

pamphlet.etymology: OE. pamflet, pamfilet, paunflet, possibly fr. OF. palme the palm of the hand, F. paume (see Palm) + OF. fueillet a leaf, dim. of fueil, m., F. feuille, f., fr. L. folium, pl. folia, thus meaning, a leaf to be held in the hand; or perh. through old French, fr. L. Pamphila, a female historian of the first century who wrote many epitomes; prob., however, fr. OF. Pamflette, the Old French name given to Pamphilus, a poem in Latin verse of the 12th century, pamphlets being named from the popularity of this poem.

panache.etymology: F., fr. L. penna a feather. See Pen a feather.

pander.etymology: From Pandarus, a leader in the Trojan army, who is represented by Chaucer and Shakespeare as having procured for Troilus the possession of Cressida.

pandiculation.etymology: L. pandiculari to stretch one's self, fr. pandere to spread out.

pandora.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Pandw`ra; pa^s, pa^n, all + dw^ron a gift.

pandurate.etymology: L. pandura a pandore + -form: cf. F. panduriforme.

panduriform.etymology: L. pandura a pandore + -form: cf. F. panduriforme.

panegyric.etymology: L. panegyricus, Gr. panhgyrico`s: cf. F. panégyrique. See Panegyric, a.

panel.etymology: Orig., a little piece; OF. panel, pannel, F. panneau, dim. of pan skirt, lappet, part or piece of a wall, side. See 2d Pane.

pang.etymology: Prob. for older prange. Cf. Prong.

panicle.etymology: L. panicula a tuft on plants, dim. of panus the thread wound upon the bobbin in a shuttle; cf. Gr. pane: cf. F. panicule. See 2d Pane.

pannier.etymology: F. panier, fr. L. panarium a bread basket, fr. panis bread. Cf. Pantry.

pantry.etymology: OE. pantrie, F. paneterie, fr. panetier pantler, LL. panetarius baker, panetus small loaf of bread, L. panis bread. Cf. Company, Pannier, Pantler.

pap.etymology: Cf. OSw. papp. Cf. Pap soft food.

papa.etymology: F. papa, L. papa; cf. Gr. Pope.

papacy.etymology: LL. papatia, fr. L. papa a father, bishop. See Pope.

papaw.etymology: Prob. from the native name in the West Indies; cf. Sp. papayo papaw, papaya the fruit of the papaw.

paper.etymology: F. papier, fr. L. papyrus papyrus, from which the Egyptians made a kind of paper, Gr. Papyrus.

par.etymology: F., fr. L. per. See Per.

parable.etymology: L. parabilis, fr. parare to provide.

parabola.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. Parable, and cf. Parabole.

parachute.etymology: F., fr. paper to ward off, guard + chute a fall. See Parry, and Chute, Chance.

parade.etymology: F., fr. Sp. parada a halt or stopping, an assembling for exercise, a place where troops are assembled to exercise, fr. parar to stop, to prepare. See Pare, v. t.

paradigm.etymology: F. paradigme, L. paradigma, fr. Gr. Para-, and Diction.

paraphernalia.etymology: LL. paraphernalia bona, fr. L. parapherna, pl., parapherna, Gr. fe`rein to bring. See 1st Bear.

parboil.etymology: OE. parboilen, OF. parbouillir to cook well; par through (see Par) + bouillir to boil, L. bullire. The sense has been influenced by E. part. See lst Boil.

parcel.etymology: F. parcelle a small part, fr. (assumed) LL. particella, dim. of L. pars. See Part, n., and cf. Particle.

parch.etymology: OE. perchen to pierce, hence used of a piercing heat or cold, OF. perchier, another form of percier, F. percer. See Pierce.

pardon.etymology: F., fr. pardonner to pardon. See Pardon, v. t.

paregoric.etymology: L. paregoricus, Gr. parégorique. See Allegory.

parent.etymology: L. parens, -entis; akin to parere to bring forth; cf. Gr. parent. Cf. Part.

parenthesis.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. Para-, En-, 2, and Thesis.

pariah.etymology: From Tamil paraiyan, pl. paraiyar, one of the low caste, fr. parai a large drum, because they beat the drums at certain festivals.

parietal.etymology: L. parietalis, fr. paries, -ietis, a wall: cf. F. pariétal. Cf. Parietary, Pellitory.

paris.etymology: From Paris, the son of Priam.

parish.etymology: OE. parishe, paresche, parosche, OF. paroisse, parosse, paroiche, F. paroisse, L. parochia, corrupted fr. paroecia, Gr. vicus village. See Vicinity, and cf. Parochial.

parity.etymology: L. paritas, fr. par, paris, equal: cf. F. parité. See Pair, Peer an equal.

park.etymology: AS. pearroc, or perh. rather fr. F. parc; both being of the same origin; cf. LL. parcus, parricus, Ir. & Gael. pairc, W. park, parwg. Cf. Paddock an inclosure, Parrock.

parlance.etymology: OF., fr. F. parler to speak. See Parley.

parley.etymology: F. parler speech, talk, fr. parler to speak, LL. parabolare, fr. L. parabola a comparison, parable, in LL., a word. See Parable, and cf. Parliament, Parlor.

parliament.etymology: OE. parlement, F. parlement, fr. parler to speak; cf. LL. parlamentum, parliamentum. See Parley.

parlor.etymology: OE. parlour, parlur, F. parloir, LL. parlatorium. See Parley.

parlous.etymology: For perlous, a contr. fr. perilous.

parochial.etymology: LL. parochialis, from L. parochia. See Parish.

parody.etymology: L. parodia, Gr. parodie. See Para- , and Ode.

parsee.etymology: Hind. & Per. parsi a Persian, a follower of Zoroaster, a fire worshiper. Cf. Persian.

parsimony.etymology: L. parsimonia, parcimonia; cf. parcere to spare, parsus sparing: cf. F. parcimonie.

parsley.etymology: OE. persely, persil, F. persil, L. petroselinum rock parsley, Gr. Celery.

parsnip.etymology: OE. parsnepe, from a French form, fr. L. pastinaca; cf. pastinare to dig up, pastinum a kind of dibble; cf. OF. pastenade, pastenaque.

parson.etymology: OE. persone person, parson, OF. persone, F. personne person, LL. persona (sc. ecclesiae), fr. L. persona a person. See Person.

part.etymology: F. part, L. pars, gen. partis; cf. parere to bring forth, produce. Cf. Parent, Depart, Parcel, Partner, Party, Portion.

parterre.etymology: F., fr. par on, by (L. per)+terre earth, ground, L. terra. See Terrace.

parthenogenesis.etymology: Gr. parqe`nos a virgin + E. genesis.

parthenon.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Parqenw`n, fr.parqe`nos a virgin, i. e., Athene, the Greek goddess called also Pallas.

partial.etymology: F., fr. LL. partials, fr. L. pars, gen. partis, a part; cf. (for sense 1) F. partiel. See Part, n.

partible.etymology: L. partibilis, fr. partire to part, divide, fr. L. pars: cf. F. partible. See Part.

participant.etymology: L. participans, p.pr. of participare: cf. F. participant. See Participate.

participate.etymology: L. participatus, p.p. of participare to participate; pars, partis, part + capere to take. See Part, and Capacious.

participial.etymology: L. participialis: cf. E. participal. See Participle.

participle.etymology: F. participe, L. participium, fr. particeps sharing, participant; pars, gen. partis, a part + capere to take. See Participate.

particle.etymology: L. particula, dim of pars, gen partis, a part: cf. F. particule. See Part, and cf. Parcel.

particular.etymology: OE. particuler, F. particulier, L. particularis. See Particle.

partisan.etymology: F., fr. It. partigiano. See Party, and cf. Partisan a truncheon.

partition.etymology: F. partition, L. partitio. See Part, v.

parturient.etymology: L. parturiens, p.pr. of parturire to desire to bring forth, fr. parere, partum, to bring forth. See Parent.

parturition.etymology: L. parturitio, fr. parturire: cf. F. parturition. See Parturient.

party.etymology: F. parti and partie, fr. F. partir to part, divide, L. partire, partiri. See Part, v.

parvenu.etymology: F., prop. p.p. of parvenir to attain to, to succeed, to rise to high station, L. pervenire to come to; per through + venire to come. See Par, prep., and Come.

parvis.etymology: F. parvis, fr. LL. paravisus, fr. L. paradisus. See Paradise.

pasch.etymology: AS. pascha, L. pascha, Gr. pesach, fr. pasach to pass over: cf. OF. pasque, F. pâque. Cf. Paschal, Paas, Paque.

pascha.etymology: AS. pascha, L. pascha, Gr. pesach, fr. pasach to pass over: cf. OF. pasque, F. pâque. Cf. Paschal, Paas, Paque.

paschal.etymology: L. paschalis: cf. F. pascal. See Pasch.

pasha.etymology: Turk. pasha, basha; cf. Per. basha, badshah; perh. a corruption of Per. padishah. Cf. Bashaw, Padishah, Shah.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

pass.etymology: F. passer, LL. passare, fr. L. passus step, or from pandere, passum, to spread out, lay open. See Pace.

passado.etymology: F. passade; cf. Sp. pasada. See Pass, v. i.

passage.etymology: F. passage. See Pass, v. i.

passant.etymology: F., p.pr. of passer. See Pass, v. i.

passenger.etymology: OE. & F. passager. See Passage, and cf. Messenger.

passeres.etymology: NL., fr. L. passer a sparrow.

passerine.etymology: L. passerinus, fr. passer a sparrow.

passiflora.etymology: NL., from L. passio passion (fr. pati, passus, to suffer) + flos, floris, flower.

passion.etymology: F., fr. L. passio, fr. pati, passus, to suffer. See Patient.

passive.etymology: L. passivus: cf. F. passif. See Passion.

passport.etymology: F. passeport, orig., a permission to leave a port or to sail into it; passer to pass + port a port, harbor. See Pass, and Port a harbor.

paste.etymology: OF. paste, F. pâte, L. pasta, fr. Gr. Pasty, n., Patty.

pastel.etymology: F.; cf. It. pastello. Cf. Pastil.

pastern.etymology: Of. pasturon, F. pâturon, fr. OF. pasture a tether, for beasts while pasturing; prop., a pasturing. See Pasture.

pastil.etymology: F. pastille, L. pastillusa pastus food. See Pasture, and cf. Pastel.

pastille.etymology: F. pastille, L. pastillusa pastus food. See Pasture, and cf. Pastel.

pastor.etymology: L., fr. pascere, pastum, to pasture, to feed. Cf. Pabulum, Pasture, Food.

pastoral.etymology: L. pastoralis: cf. F. pastoral. See Pastor.

pasturage.etymology: OF. pasturage, F. pâturage. See Pasture.

pasture.etymology: OF. pasture, F. pâture, L. pastura, fr. pascere, pastum, to pasture, to feed. See Pastor.

pasty.etymology: OF. pasté, F. pâté. See Paste, and cf. Patty.

pat.etymology: Cf. G. patschen, Prov. G. patzen, to strike, tap.

patch.etymology: OE. pacche; of uncertain origin, perh. for placche; cf. Prov. E. platch patch, LG. plakk, plakke.

patchouli.etymology: CF. F. patchouli; prob. of East Indian origin.

patchouly.etymology: CF. F. patchouli; prob. of East Indian origin.

patella.etymology: L., a small pan, the kneepan, dim. of patina, patena, a pan, dish.

patent.etymology: L. patens, -entis, p.pr. of patere to be open: cf. F. patent. Cf. Fathom.

paterfamilias.etymology: L., fr. pater father + familias, gen. of familia family.

paternal.etymology: L. paternus, fr. pater a father: cf. F. paternel. See Father.

paternity.etymology: L. paternitas: cf. F. paternité. See Paternal.

path.etymology: As. pad, G. pfad, of uncertain origin; cf. Gr. patha, path. sq. root21.

pathetic.etymology: L. patheticus, Gr. pathétique. See Pathos.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

pathos.etymology: L., from Gr. pati to suffer, E. patient.

patience.etymology: F. patience, fr. L. patientia. See Patient.

patient.etymology: F., fr. L. patiens, -entis, p.pr. of pati to suffer. Cf. Pathos, Passion.

patina.etymology: It., fr. L. patina a dish, a pan, a kind of cake. Cf. Paten.

patrial.etymology: L. patria fatherland, country, fr. pater father.

patriarch.etymology: F. patriarche, L. patriarcha, Gr. Father, Archaic.

patrician.etymology: L. patricius, fr. patres fathers or senators, pl. of pater: cf. F. patricien. See Paternal.

patricide.etymology: L. pater father + caedere to kill. Cf. Parricide.

patrimony.etymology: L. patrimonium, fr. pater father: cf. F. patrimoine. See Paternal.

patriot.etymology: F. patriote; cf. Sp. patriota, It. patriotto; all fr. Gr. Father.

patrol.etymology: F. patrouiller, O. & Prov. F. patrouiller to paddle, paw about, patrol, fr. patte a paw; cf. D. poot paw, G. pfote, and E. pat, v.

patron.etymology: F., fr. L. patronus, fr. pater a father. See Paternal, and cf. Patroon, Padrone, Pattern.

patronage.etymology: F. patronage. Cf. LL. patronaticum, and L. patronatus.

patten.etymology: F. patin a high-heeled shoe, fr. patte paw, foot. Cf. Panton, Patté.

patter.etymology: Freq. of pat to strike gently.

pattern.etymology: OE. patron, F. patron, a patron, also, a pattern. See Patron.

paucity.etymology: L. paucitas, fr. paucus few, little: cf. F. paucité See Few.

paunch.etymology: OF. panch, pance, F. panse, L. pantex, panticis.

roots.meaning: A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

pause.etymology: F., fr. L. pausa. See Pose.

pavan.etymology: F. pavane; cf. It. & Sp. pavana, and Sp. pavon, pavo, a peacock, L. pavo.

pave.etymology: F., from paver to pave. See Pave.

pavement.etymology: F., fr. LL. pavamentum, L. pavimentum. See Pave.

pavilion.etymology: F. pavillon, fr. L. pavilio a butterfly, also, a tent, because spread out like a butterfly's wings.

pavise.etymology: OF. pavaix, F. pavois; cf. It. pavese, LL. pavense; perh. named from Pavia in Italy.

paw.etymology: OE. pawe, poue, OF. poe: cf. patte, LG. pote, D. poot, G. pfote.

pawl.etymology: W. pawl a pole, a stake. Cf. Pole a stake.

pawn.etymology: OE. paune, poun, OF. peon, poon, F. pion, LL. pedo a foot soldier, fr. L. pes, pedis, foot. See Foot, and cf. Pioneer, Peon.

pay.etymology: OF. peier, fr. L. picare to pitch, i pitch: cf. OF. peiz pitch, F. poix. See Pitch a black substance.

payment.etymology: F. payment, paiement. See Pay to requite.

peace.etymology: OE. pees, pais, OF. pais, paiz, pes, F. paix, L. pax, pacis, akin to pacere, paciscere, pacisci, to make an agreement, and prob. also pangere to fasten. Cf. Appease, Fair, a., Fay, v., Fang, Pacify, Pact, Pay to requite.

peacock.etymology: OE. pecok. Pea- in this word is from AS. peá, pawa, peacock, fr. L. pavo, prob. of Oriental origin; cf. Gr. taus, tawus, Ar. tawu. See Cock the bird.

peak.etymology: OE. pek, AS. peac, perh of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. peac a sharp-pointed thing. Cf. Pike.

pear.etymology: OE. pere, AS. peru, L. pirum: cf. F. poire. Cf. Perry.

pearl.etymology: OE. perle, F. perle, LL. perla, perula, probably fr. (assumed) L. pirulo, dim. of L. pirum a pear. See Pear, and cf. Purl to mantle.

peasant.etymology: OF. païsant (the i being perh. due to confusion with the p.pr. of verbs), païsan, F. paysan, fr. OF. & F. pays country, fr. L. pagus the country. See Pagan.

pebble.etymology: AS. papolstan; cf. L. papula pimple, mote. See Stone.

peccadillo.etymology: Sp. pecadillo, dim. of pecado a sin, fr. L. peccatum. See Peccant.

peccant.etymology: L. peccans, -antis, p.pr. of peccare to sin: cf. F. peccant.

peccary.etymology: From the native South American name: cf. F. pécari, Sp. pecar.

peck.etymology: Perh. akin to pack; or, orig., an indefinite quantity, and fr. peck, v. (below): cf. also F. picotin a peak.

pectinate.etymology: L. pectinatus, p.pr. of pectinare to comb, from pecten, -inis, a comb; cf. Gr. feax hair, OHG. fahs, E. paxwax.

pectoral.etymology: L. pectoralis, fr. pectus, -oris the breast; cf. F. pectoral.

peculate.etymology: L. peculatus, p.p. of peculari to peculate, akin to peculium private property. See Peculiar.

peculiar.etymology: L. peculiaris, fr. peculium private property, akin to pecunia money: cf. OF. peculier. See Pecuniary.

pecuniary.etymology: L. pecuniarius, fr. pecunia money, orig., property in cattle, fr. pecus cattle: cf. F. pécuniaire. See Fee, and cf. Peculiar.

pedagogic.etymology: From Pedagogic, a.; cf. G. pedagogik.

pedagogue.etymology: F. pédagogue, L. paedagogus, Gr. Page a servant, Agent.

pedal.etymology: L. pedalis, fr. pes, pedis, foot. See Foot, and cf. Pew.

pedant.etymology: F. pédant, It. pedante, fr. Gr. pai^s boy. See Pedagogue.

pedate.etymology: L. pedatus, p.p. of pedare to furnish with feet, fr. pes, pedis, a foot.

peddler.etymology: OE. pedlere, pedlare, also peddare, peoddare, fr. OE. ped a basket, of unknown origin.

pederast.etymology: Gr. paiderasth`s; pai^s, paido`s, a boy + 'era^n to love: cf. F. pédéraste.

pedestal.etymology: Sp. pedestal; cf. F. piédestal, It. piedestallo; fr. L. es, pedis, foot + OHG. stal standing place, station, place, akin to E. stall. See Foot, and Stall, and Footstall.

pedicle.etymology: L. pediculus a little foot, dim. of pes foot: cf. F. pédicule. See edal, and cf. Pedicel.

pedigree.etymology: Of unknown origin; possibly fr. F. par degrés by degrees, -- for a pedigree is properly a genealogical table which records the relationship of families by degrees; or, perh., fr. F. pied de grue crane's foot, from the shape of the heraldic genealogical trees.

pediment.etymology: L. pes, pedis, a foot. See Foot.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
Combining forms from L. pes, pedis, foot, as pedipalp, pedireme, pedometer.

A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

peduncle.etymology: Formed fr. (assumed) L. pedunculus, dim. of pes, pedis, a foot: cf. F. pédoncule.

peek.etymology: OE. piken: cf. F. piquer to pierce, prick, E. pique. Cf. Peak.

peel.etymology: OE. pel. Cf. Pile a heap.

peen.etymology: Cf. G. pinne pane of a hammer.

peep.etymology: Of imitative origin; cf. OE. pipen, F. piper, pépier, L. pipire, pipare, pipiare, D. & G. piepen. Senses 2 and 3 perhaps come from a transfer of sense from the sound which chickens make upon the first breaking of the shell to the act accompanying it; or perhaps from the influence of peek, or peak. Cf. Pipe.

peer.etymology: OF. parir, pareir equiv. to F. paraître to appear, L. parere. Cf. Appear.

peerage.etymology: See Peer an equal, and cf. Parage.

peevish.etymology: OE. pevische; of uncertain origin, perh. from a word imitative of the noise made by fretful children + -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

peg.etymology: OE. pegge; cf. Sw. pigg, Dan. pig a point, prickle, and E. peak.

peignoir.etymology: F., fr. peigner to comb, L. pectinare. See Pectinate.

pejorative.etymology: F. péjoratif, fr. L. pejor, used as compar. of malus evil.

pelage.etymology: F. pelage, fr. L. pilus hair.

pelf.etymology: OE. pelfir booty, OF. pelfre, akin to pelfrer to plunder, and perh. to E. pillage. Cf. Pilfer.

pelican.etymology: F. pélican, L. pelicanus, pelecanus, Gr. paraçu.

pelisse.etymology: F., fr. L. pelliceus, pellicius, made of skins, fr. pellis a skin. Cf. Pelt skin, Pilch, and see 2d Pell.

pellet.etymology: F. pelote, LL. pelota, pilota, fr. L. pila a ball. Cf. Platoon.

pellicle.etymology: L. pellicu, dim. of pellis skin: cf. F. pellicule.

pellitory.etymology: OE. paritorie, OF. paritoire, F. pariétaire; (cf. It. & Sp. parietaria), L. parietaria the parietary, or pellitory, the wall plant, fr. parietarus belonging to the walls, fr. paries, parietis a wall. Cf. Parietary.

pellucid.etymology: L. pellucidus; per (see Per-) + lucidus clear, bright: cf. F. pellucide.

roots.meaning: Originally, denoting that the element to the name of which it is prefixed in the respective compounds exercised its highest valence; now, only that the element has a higher valence than in other similar compounds; thus, barium peroxide is the highest oxide of barium; while nitrogen and manganese peroxides, so-called, are not the highest oxides of those elements.

pelt.etymology: Cf. G. pelz a pelt, fur, fr. OF. pelice, F. pelisse (see Pelisse); or perh. shortened fr. peltry.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

pen.etymology: OE. penne, OF. penne, pene, F. penne, fr. L. penna.

penal.etymology: L. poenalis, fr. poena punishment: cf. F. pénal. See Pain.

penance.etymology: OF. penance, peneance, L. paenitentia repentance. See Penitence.

penchant.etymology: F., fr. pencher to bend, fr. (assumed) LL. pendicare, L. pendere. See Pendant.

pencil.etymology: OF. pincel, F. pinceau, L. penicillum, penicillus, equiv. to peniculus, dim. of penis a tail. Cf. Penicil.

pendant.etymology: F., orig. p.pr. of pendre to hang, L. pendere. Cf. Pendent, Pansy, Pensive, Poise, Ponder.

pendent.etymology: L. pendens, -entis, p.pr. of pendere to hang, to be suspended. Cf. Pendant.

pending.etymology: L. pendere to hang, to be suspended. Cf. Pendent.

pendulous.etymology: L. pendulus, fr. pendere to hang. Cf. Pendant, and cf. Pendulum.

pendulum.etymology: NL., fr. L. pendulus hanging, swinging. See Pendulous.

peneplain.etymology: L. paene, pene, almost + E. plain.

penetralia.etymology: L., fr. penetralis penetrating, internal. See Penetrate.

penetrate.etymology: L. penetratus, p.p. of penetrare to penetrate; akin to penitus inward, inwardly, and perh. to pens with, in the power of, penus store of food, innermost part of a temple.

penguin.etymology: Perh. orig. the name of another bird, and fr. W. pen head + gwyn white; or perh. from a native South American name.

peninsula.etymology: L. peninsula or paeninsula; paene almost + insula an island. See Isle.

penitence.etymology: F. pénitence, L. paenitentia. See Penitent, and cf. Penance.

penitent.etymology: F. pénitent, L. paenitens, -entis, poenitens, p.pr. of paenitere, poenitere, to cause to repent, to repent; prob. akin to poena punishment. See Pain.

pennant.etymology: OE. penon, penoun, pynoun, OF. penon, F. pennon, fr. L. penna feather. See Pen a feather, and cf. Pennon, Pinion.

pennate.etymology: L. pennatus feathered, winged, from penna feather, wing.

pennatula.etymology: NL., fr. L. penna a feather.

penny.etymology: Perh. a corruption of pun, for pound.

pennyroyal.etymology: A corruption of OE. puliall royal. OE. puliall is ultimately derived fr. L. puleium, or pulegium regium (so called as being good against fleas), fr. pulex a flea; and royal is a translation of L. regium, in puleium regium.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

pension.etymology: F., fr. L. pensio a paying, payment, fr. pendere, pensum, to weight, to pay; akin to pend to hang. See Pendant, and cf. Spend.

pensive.etymology: F. pensif, fr. penser to think, fr. L. pensare to weigh, ponder, consider, v. intens. fr. pendere to weigh. See Pension, Poise.

penstock.etymology: Etymol. uncertain; perh. fr. pen an inclosure + stock.

pentagon.etymology: Gr. Penta-) + gwni`a angle: cf. L. pentagonium, F. pentagone.

pentateuch.etymology: L. pentateuchus, Gr. Penta-) + text. See Five, and Text.

pentavalent.etymology: Penta- + L. valens, p. pr. See Valence.

pentecost.etymology: L. pentecoste, Gr. Five, and cf. Pingster.

penultima.etymology: L. (sc. syllaba), fr. penultimus, paenultimus, the last but one; paene almost + ultimus the last.

penumbra.etymology: NL., fr. L. paene almost + umbra shade.

peon.etymology: Sp. peon, or Pg. pe, one who travels on foot, a foot soldier, a pawn in chess. See Pawn in chess.

peony.etymology: OE. pione, pioine, pioni, OF. pione, F. pivoine, L. paeonia, Gr. Pæan.

people.etymology: From Middle English puple , peple , peeple , from Anglo-Norman people , from Old French pueple , peuple , pople , from Latin populus ( “ a people, nation ” ) , from Old Latin populus , from earlier poplus , from even earlier poplos , from Proto-Italic *poplos ( “ army ” ) of unknown origin. Doublet of pueblo . Gradually ousted native English lede and, partially, folk .

pepper.etymology: OE. peper, AS. pipor, L. piper, fr. Gr. pippala, pippali.

peradventure.etymology: OE. per aventure, F. par aventure. See Per, and Adventure.

perambulate.etymology: L. perambulatus, p.p. of perambulare to perambulate; per through + ambulare to walk. See Per-, and Amble.

roots.meaning: Originally, denoting that the element to the name of which it is prefixed in the respective compounds exercised its highest valence; now, only that the element has a higher valence than in other similar compounds; thus, barium peroxide is the highest oxide of barium; while nitrogen and manganese peroxides, so-called, are not the highest oxides of those elements.

perceive.etymology: OF. percevoir, perceveir, L. percipere, perceptum; per (see Per-) + capere to take, receive. See Capacious, and cf. Perception.

roots.meaning: Originally, denoting that the element to the name of which it is prefixed in the respective compounds exercised its highest valence; now, only that the element has a higher valence than in other similar compounds; thus, barium peroxide is the highest oxide of barium; while nitrogen and manganese peroxides, so-called, are not the highest oxides of those elements.

percentage.etymology: Per cent + -age, as in average. See Per, and Cent.

perceptible.etymology: L. perceptibilis: cf. F. perceptible. See Perceive.

perception.etymology: L. perceptio: cf. F. perception. See Perceive.

perch.etymology: OE. perche, F. perche, L. perca, fr. Gr. p spotted, speckled, and E. freckle.

perchance.etymology: F. par by (L. per) + chance. See Par, and Chance.

percipient.etymology: L. percipiens, -entis, p.pr. of percipere. See Perceive.

percoid.etymology: L. perca a perch + -oid: cf. F. percoïde.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

percolate.etymology: L. percolatus, p.p. of percolare to percolate; per through + colare to strain.

percuss.etymology: L. percussus, p.p. of percutere; per + quatere to shake, strike. See Quash.

percussion.etymology: L. percussio: cf. F. percussion. See Percuss.

perdition.etymology: F., fr. L. perditio, fr. perdere, perditum, to ruin, to lose; per (cf. Skr. para away) + -dere (only in comp.) to put; akin to Gr. do. See Do.

pickax.etymology: A corruption of OE. pikois, pikeis, F. picois, fr. pic. See Pick, n.

pickaxe.etymology: A corruption of OE. pikois, pikeis, F. picois, fr. pic. See Pick, n.

picket.etymology: F. piquet, properly dim. of pique spear, pike. See Pike, and cf. Piquet.

pickle.etymology: Cf. D. pekel. Probably a dim. fr. Pick, v. t., alluding to the cleaning of the fish.

picnic.etymology: Cf. F. piquenique. See Pick, v., and cf. Knickknack.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

pictorial.etymology: L. pictorius, fr. pictor a painter, fr. pingere to paint. See Paint.

picture.etymology: L. pictura, fr. pingere, pictum, to paint: cf. F. peinture. See Paint.

picturesque.etymology: It. pittoresco: cf. F. pittoresque. See Pictorial.

picul.etymology: Jav. & Malay pikul, fr. pikul to carry on the back, to carry a burden; n., a man's burden.

piddle.etymology: Cf. dial. Sw. pittla to keep picking at, Sw. peta to pick.

pie.etymology: OE. pie, pye; cf. Ir. & Gael. pighe pie, also Gael. pige an earthen jar or pot. Cf. Piggin.

piece.etymology: OE. pece, F. pièce, LL. pecia, petia, petium, probably of Celtic origin; cf. W. peth a thing, a part, portion, a little, Armor. pez, Gael. & Ir. cuid part, share. Cf. Petty.

piecemeal.etymology: OE. pecemele; pece a piece + AS. m, dat. pl. of m part. See Meal a portion.

pier.etymology: OE. pere, OF. piere a stone, F. pierre, fr. L. petra, Gr. Petrify.

pierce.etymology: OE. percen, F. percer, OF. percier, perchier, parchier; perh. fr. (assumed) LL. pertusiare for pertusare, fr. L. pertundere, pertusum, to beat, push, bore through; per through + tundere to beat: cf. OF. pertuisier to pierce, F. pertuis a hole. Cf. Contuse, Parch, Pertuse.

piety.etymology: F. piété; cf. It. pietà; both fr. L. pietas piety, fr. pius pious. See Pious, and cf. Pity.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

pig.etymology: Cf. D. big, bigge, LG. bigge, also Dan. pige girl, Sw. piga, Icel. pika.

pigeon.etymology: F., fr. L. pipio a young pipping or chirping bird, fr. pipire to peep, chirp. Cf. Peep to chirp.

pigment.etymology: L. pigmentum, fr. the root of pingere to paint: cf. F. pigment. See Paint, and cf. Pimento, Orpiment.

pike.etymology: F. pique; perhaps of Celtic origin; cf. W. pig a prick, a point, beak, Arm. pik pick. But cf. also L. picus woodpecker (see Pie magpie), and E. spike. Cf. Pick, n. & v., Peak, Pique.

pilaster.etymology: F. pilastre, It. pilastro, LL. pilastrum, fr. L. pila a pillar. See Pillar.

pilchard.etymology: Cf. It. pilseir, W. pilcod minnows.

piles.etymology: L. pila a ball. Cf. Pill a medicine.

pilgrim.etymology: OE. pilgrim, pelgrim, pilegrim, pelegrim; cf. D. pelgrim, OHG. piligrim, G. pilger, F. pèlerin, It. pellegrino; all fr. L. peregrinus a foreigner, fr. pereger abroad; per through + ager land, field. See Per-, and Acre, and cf. Pelerine, Peregrine.

roots.meaning: Originally, denoting that the element to the name of which it is prefixed in the respective compounds exercised its highest valence; now, only that the element has a higher valence than in other similar compounds; thus, barium peroxide is the highest oxide of barium; while nitrogen and manganese peroxides, so-called, are not the highest oxides of those elements.

pilgrimage.etymology: OE. pilgrimage, pelgrinage; cf. F. pèlerinage.

pillage.etymology: F., fr. piller to plunder. See Pill to plunder.

pillar.etymology: OE. pilerF. pilier, LL. pilare, pilarium, pilarius, fr. L. pila a pillar. See Pile a heap.

pillion.etymology: Ir. pillin, pilliun (akin to Gael. pillean, pillin), fr. Ir. & Gael. pill, peall, a skin or hide, prob. fr. L. pellis. See Pell, n., Fell skin.

pillory.etymology: F. pilori; cf. Pr. espitlori, LL. piloricum, pilloricum, pellericum, pellorium, pilorium, spilorium; perhaps from a derivative of L. speculari to look around, observe. Cf. Speculate.

pillow.etymology: OE. pilwe, AS. pyle, fr. L. pilvinus.

pilocarpine.etymology: From NL. Pilocarpus pennatifolius jaborandi; L. pilus hair + Gr. pilocarpine.

pilose.etymology: L. pilosus, fr. pilus hair. See Pile.

pilot.etymology: F. pilote, prob. from D. peillood plummet, sounding lead; peilen, pegelen, to sound, measure (fr. D. & G. peil, pegel, a sort of measure, water mark) + lood lead, akin to E. lead. The pilot, then, is the lead man, i.e., he who throws the lead. See Pail, and Lead a metal.

pimento.etymology: Sp. pimiento, pimienta; cf. Pg. pimenta, F. piment; all fr. L. pigmentum a paint, pigment, the juice of plants; hence, something spicy and aromatic. See Pigment.

pimp.etymology: Cf. F. pimpant smart, sparkish; perh. akin to piper to pipe, formerly also, to excel. Cf. Pipe.

pimpernel.etymology: F. pimprenelle; cf. Sp. pimpinela, It. pimpinella; perh. from LL. bipinnella, for bipinnula two-winged, equiv. to L. bipennis; bis twice + penna feather, wing. Cf. Pen a feather.

pimple.etymology: AS. pipelian to blister; cf. L. papula pimple.

pin.etymology: Cf. Pen to confine, or Pinfold.

pinch.etymology: F. pincer, probably fr. OD. pitsen to pinch; akin to G. pfetzen to cut, pinch; perhaps of Celtic origin. Cf. Piece.

pinchbeck.etymology: Said to be from the name of the inventor; cf. It. prencisbecco.

pindaric.etymology: L. Pindaricus, Gr. Pindarus) Pindar: cf. F. pindarique.

pine.etymology: AS. pin, L. poena penalty. See Pain.

pineal.etymology: L. pinea the cone of a pine, from pineus of the pine, from pinus a pine: cf. F. pinéale.

pinfish.etymology: So called from their sharp dorsal spines.

pinfold.etymology: For pindfold. See Pinder, Pound an inclosure, and Fold an inclosure.

pinguicula.etymology: NL., fr. L. pinguiculus somewhat fat, fattish.

pinion.etymology: OF. pignon a pen, F., gable, pinion (in sense 5); cf. Sp. piñon pinion; fr. L. pinna pinnacle, feather, wing. See Pin a peg, and cf. Pen a feather, Pennat, Pennon.

pinite.etymology: So called from Pini, a mine in Saxony.

pinnace.etymology: F. pinasse; cf. It. pinassa, pinazza, Sp. pinaza; all from L. pinus a pine tree, anything made of pine, e.g., a ship. Cf. Pine a tree.

pinnacle.etymology: OE. pinacle, F. pinacle, L. pinnaculum, fr. pinna pinnacle, feather. See Pin a peg.

pinnate.etymology: L. pinnatus feathered, fr. pinna a feather. See Pin a peg, Pen feather.

pinnated.etymology: L. pinnatus feathered, fr. pinna a feather. See Pin a peg, Pen feather.

pinnatifid.etymology: L. pinnatus feathered + root of findere to split: cf. F. pinnatifide.

pinnatiped.etymology: L. pinnatus feathered + pes, pedis foot: cf. F. pinnatipède.

pinniped.etymology: L. pinna feather, fin + pes, pedis, a foot: cf. F. pinnipède.

pinnipedia.etymology: NL. So called because their webbed feet are used as paddles or fins.

pinnule.etymology: L. pinnula, dim. of pinna feather: cf. F. pinnule.

pint.etymology: OE. pinte, F. pinte, fr. Sp. pinta spot, mark, pint, fr. pintar to paint; a mark for a pint prob. having been made on or in a larger measure. See Paint.

pintado.etymology: Sp., painted, fr. pintar to paint.

pioneer.etymology: F. pionier, orig., a foot soldier, OF. peonier, fr. OF. peon a foot soldier, F. pion. See Pawn in chess.

pip.etymology: OE. pippe, D. pip, or F. pépie; from LL. pipita, fr. L. pituita slime, phlegm, rheum, in fowls, the pip. Cf. Pituite.

pipe.etymology: AS. pipe, probably fr. L. pipare, pipire, to chirp; of imitative origin. Cf. Peep, Pibroch, Fife.

piperine.etymology: L. piper pepper: cf. F. piperin, piperine.

pipit.etymology: So named from its call note.

pippin.etymology: Probably fr. OE. pippin a seed, as being raised from the seed. See Pip a seed.

piquant.etymology: F., p.pr. of piquer to prick or sting. See Pike.

pique.etymology: F., p.p. of piquer to prick.

piquet.etymology: F., prob. fr. pique. See Pique, Pike, and Picket.

pirate.etymology: L. pirata, Gr. peril: cf. F. pirate. See Peril.

pirogue.etymology: Originally an American Indian word: cf. F. pirogue, Sp. piroga, piragua.

piscary.etymology: L. piscarius relating to fishes or to fishing, fr. piscis a fish.

piscatorial.etymology: L. piscatorius, fr. piscator a fisherman, fr. piscari to fish, fr. piscis a fish. See Fish the animal.

piscatory.etymology: L. piscatorius, fr. piscator a fisherman, fr. piscari to fish, fr. piscis a fish. See Fish the animal.

piscivorous.etymology: L. piscis a fish + vorare to devour: cf. F. piscivore.

pisiform.etymology: L. pisum a pea + -form: cf. F. pisiforme.

pismire.etymology: Piss + mire; so called because it discharges a moisture vulgarly considered urine. See Mire an ant.

piss.etymology: OE. pissen, F. pisser; akin to It. pisciare, D. & G. pissen, Dan. pisse, Icel. pissa.

pistachio.etymology: It. pistacchio (cf. Sp. pistacho, F. pistache), fr. L. pistacium, Gr. pistah. Cf. Fistinut.

piste.etymology: F., fr. L. pisere, pinsere, pistum, to pound.

pistil.etymology: L. pistillum, pistillus, a pestle: cf. F. pistil. See Pestle.

pistol.etymology: F. pistole, pistolet, It. pistola; prob. from a form Pistola, for Pistoja, a town in Italy where pistols were first made. Cf. Pistole.

piston.etymology: F. piston; cf. It. pistone piston, also pestone a large pestle; all fr. L. pinsere, pistum, to pound, to stamp. See Pestle, Pistil.

pit.etymology: OE. pit, put, AS. pytt a pit, hole, L. puteus a well, pit.

pitahaya.etymology: Sp., prob. from the native name.

pitcher.etymology: OE. picher, OF. pichier, OHG. pehhar, pehhari; prob. of the same origin as E. beaker. Cf. Beaker.

piteous.etymology: OE. pitous, OF. pitos, F. piteux. See Pity.

pith.etymology: AS. pi; akin to D. pit pith, kernel, LG. peddik. Cf. Pit a kernel.

pittance.etymology: OE. pitance, pitaunce, F. pitance; cf. It. pietanza, LL. pitancia, pittantia, pictantia; perh. fr. L. pietas pity, piety, or perhaps akin to E. petty. Cf. Petty, and Pity.

pituitary.etymology: L. pituita phlegm, pituite: cf. F. pituitarie.

pity.etymology: OE. pite, OF. pité, pitié, F. pitié, L. pietas piety, kindness, pity. See Pious, and cf. Piety.

pivot.etymology: F.; prob. akin to It. piva pipe, F. pipe. See Pipe.

placable.etymology: L. placabilis, fr. placare to quiet, pacify: cf. F. placable. See Placate.

placard.etymology: F., fr. plaquer to lay or clap on, plaque plate, tablet; probably from Dutch, cf. D. plakken to paste, post up, plak a flat piece of wood.

placate.etymology: L. placatus, p.p. of placare to placate, akin to placere to please. See Please.

place.etymology: F., fr. L. platea a street, an area, a courtyard, from Gr. platei^a a street, properly fem. of platy`s, flat, broad; akin to Skr. prsthu, Lith. platus. Cf. Flawn, Piazza, Plate, Plaza.

placebo.etymology: L., I shall please, fut. of placere to please.

placid.etymology: L. placidus, originally, pleasing, mild, from placere to please: cf. F. placide. See Please.

placket.etymology: F. plaquer to lay or clap on. See Placard.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

plague.etymology: L. plaga a blow, stroke, plague; akin to Gr. plangere to strike, beat. Cf. Plaint.

plaice.etymology: F. plaise, plais, prob. fr. L. platessa flatish, plaice. See Place.

plaid.etymology: Gael. plaide a blanket or plaid, contr. fr. peallaid a sheepskin, fr. peall a skin or hide. CF. Pillion.

plain.etymology: OE. playne, pleyne, fr. F. plaindre. See Plaint.

plaint.etymology: OE. plainte, pleynte, F. plainte, fr. L. plangere, planctum (plancta, fem. p.p.), to beat, beat the breast, lament. Cf. Complain, Plague, Plangent.

plaintiff.etymology: F. plaintif making complaint, plaintive; in Old French equiv. to plaignant complainant, prosecutor, fr. plaindre. See Plaint, and cf. Plaintive.

plait.etymology: OE. playte, OF. pleit, L. plicatum, plicitum, p.p. of plicare to fold, akin to plectere to plait. See Ply, and cf. Plat to weave, Pleat, Plight fold.

plan.etymology: F., fr. L. planus flat, level. See Plain, a.

planchet.etymology: F. planchette a small board, dim. of planche. See Planch.

plane.etymology: F., fr. L. platanus, Gr. Place, and cf. Platane, Plantain the tree.

planetarium.etymology: NL.: cf. F. planétaire. See Planetary.

planetary.etymology: Cf. L. planetarius an astrologer, F. planétaire planetary. See Planet.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

plangent.etymology: L. plangens, -entis, fr. plangere to beat. See Plaint.

roots.meaning: Combining forms signifying flat, level, plane; as planifolious, planimetry, plano-concave.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

plank.etymology: OE. planke, OF. planque, planche, F. planche, fr. L. planca; cf. Gr. Planch.

plantain.etymology: Cf. F. plantain-arbre, plantanier, Sp. plántano, plátano; prob. same word as plane tree.

plantar.etymology: L. plantaris, fr. planta the sole of the foot.

plantigrade.etymology: L. planta sole of the foot + gradi to walk: cf. F. plantigrade.

plaque.etymology: F. Cf. Plack, and see Placard.

plasm.etymology: L. plasma anything formed or molded, that which is molded, Gr. plasme. Cf. Plasma.

plaster.etymology: AS., a plaster (in sense 1), fr. L. emplastrum, Gr. plastre a plaster (in sense 2), F. plâtre. Cf. Plastic, Emplaster, Piaster.

plastron.etymology: F. plastron breastplate, plastron, LL. plastra a thin plate of metal. See Plaster.

platan.etymology: L. platanus. See Plane the tree.

plate.etymology: OF. plate a plate of metal, a cuirsas, F. plat a plate, a shallow vessel of silver, other metal, or earth, fr. plat flat, Gr. Place, n.

plateau.etymology: F., fr. OF. platel, properly a little plate. See Plate.

platen.etymology: F. platine, fr. plat flat. See Plate, and cf. Platin.

platinum.etymology: NL., fr. Sp. platina, from plata silver, LL. plata a thin plate of metal. See Plate, and cf. Platina.

platitude.etymology: F., from plat flat. See Plate.

platoon.etymology: F. peloton a ball of thread, a knot or group of men, a platoon, from pelote a ball formed of things wound round. See Pellet.

plaudit.etymology: From L. plaudite do ye praise (which was said by players at the end of a performance), 2d pers. pl. imperative of plaudere. Cf. Plausible.

plausible.etymology: L. plausibilis praiseworthy, from plaudere, plausum, to applaud, clap the hands, strike, beat.

play.etymology: OE. pleien, AS. plegian, plegan, to play, akin to plega play, game, quick motion, and probably to OS. plegan to promise, pledge, D. plegen to care for, attend to, be wont, G. pflegen; of unknown origin. sq. root28. Cf. Plight, n.

plea.etymology: OE. plee, plai, plait, fr. OF. plait, plaid, plet, LL. placitum judgment, decision, assembly, court, fr. L. placitum that which is pleasing, an opinion, sentiment, from placere to please. See Please, and cf. Placit, Plead.

pleach.etymology: Cf. OF. plaissier to bend, and also F. plisser to plait, L. plicare, plicitum, to fold, lay, or wind together. Cf. Plash to pleach.

plead.etymology: OE. pleden, plaiden, OF. plaidier, F. plaider, fr. LL. placitare, fr. placitum. See Plea.

please.etymology: OE. plesen, OF. plaisir, fr. L. placere, akin to placare to reconcile. Cf. Complacent, Placable, Placid, Plea, Plead, Pleasure.

pleasure.etymology: F. plaisir, originally an infinitive. See Please.

plebeian.etymology: L. plebeius, from plebs, plebis, the common people: cf. F. plébéien.

pledge.etymology: OF. plege, pleige, pledge, guaranty, LL. plegium, plivium; akin to OF. plevir to bail, guaranty, perhaps fr. L. praebere to proffer, offer (sc. fidem a trust, a promise of security), but cf. also E. play. sq. root28. Cf. Prebend, Replevin.

plenary.etymology: LL. plenarius, fr. L. plenus full. See Plenty.

plenitude.etymology: L. plenitudo, fr. plenus full; cf. F. plenitude.

plenty.etymology: OE. plentee, plente, OF. plenté, fr. L. plenitas, fr. plenus full. See Full, a., and cf. Complete.

pleonasm.etymology: L. pleonasmus, Gr. Full, a., and cf. Poly-, Plus.

roots.meaning: A combining form or prefix from Gr. poly`s, many; as, polygon, a figure of many angles; polyatomic, having many atoms; polychord, polyconic.
A combining form or suffix from Gr. poy`s, podo`s, foot; as, decapod, an animal having ten feet; phyllopod, an animal having leaflike feet; myriapod, hexapod.
A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

pleurisy.etymology: F. pleurésie, L. pleurisis, pleuritis, Gr pleyri is (sc. no`sos), fr. pleyra` rib, side.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting relation to a side; specif., connection with, or situation in or near, the pleura; as, pleuroperitoneum.
A combining form denoting relation to a side; specif., connection with, or situation in or near, the pleura; as, pleuroperitoneum.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

plexus.etymology: L., a twining, braid, fr. plectere, plexum, to twine, braid.

pliable.etymology: F., fr. plier to bend, to fold. See Ply, v.

pliant.etymology: F. pliant, p. pr. of plier to bend. See Ply, v.

plica.etymology: LL., a fold, fr. L. plicare to fold. See Ply, v.

plicate.etymology: L. plicatus, p. p. of plicare to fold.

plight.etymology: OE. pliten; probably through Old French, fr. LL. plectare, L. plectere. See Plait, Ply.

plinth.etymology: L. plinthus, Gr. flint: cf. F. plinthe.

plod.etymology: Gf. Gael. plod a clod, a pool; also, to strike or pelt with a clod or clods.

plot.etymology: AS. plot; cf. Goth. plats a patch. Cf. Plat a piece of ground.

plough.etymology: OE. plouh, plou, AS. ploh; akin to D. ploeg, G. pflug, OHG. pfluog, pfluoh, Icel. plogr, Sw. plog, Dan. ploug, plov, Russ. plug', Lith. plugas.

plover.etymology: OF. plovier, F. pluvier, prop., the rain bird, fr. LL. (assumed) pluviarius, fr. L. pluvia rain, from pluere to rain; akin to E. float, G. fliessen to flow. See Float.

plow.etymology: OE. plouh, plou, AS. ploh; akin to D. ploeg, G. pflug, OHG. pfluog, pfluoh, Icel. plogr, Sw. plog, Dan. ploug, plov, Russ. plug', Lith. plugas.

plug.etymology: Akin to D. plug, G. pflock, Dan. plök, plug, Sw. plugg; cf. W. ploc.

plum.etymology: AS.plume, fr. L. prunum; akin to Gr. Prune a dried plum.

plumb.etymology: F. plomb, L. plumbum lead, a leaden ball or bullet; cf. Gr. Plummet, Plunge.

plume.etymology: F., fr. L. pluma. Cf. Fly, v.

plummet.etymology: OE. plommet, OF. plommet, fr. plom, plum, lead, F. plomb. See Plumb.

plumose.etymology: L. plumosus, fr. pluma feather: cf. F. plumeux.

plump.etymology: OE. plomp rude, clumsy; akin to D. plomp, G., Dan., & Sw. plump; probably of imitative origin. Cf. Plump, adv.

plumule.etymology: L. plumula, dim. of pluma a feather; cf. F. plumule.

plunder.etymology: G. plündern to plunder, plunder frippery, baggage.

plunge.etymology: OE. ploungen, OF. plongier, F. plonger, fr. (assumed) LL. plumbicare, fr. L. plumbum lead. See Plumb.

pluperfect.etymology: L. plus more + perfectus perfect; cf. F. plus-que-parfait, L. plusquamperfectum.

plural.etymology: L. pluralis, from plus, pluris, more; cf. F. pluriel, OF. plurel. See Plus.

plus.etymology: L., more; akin to Gr. full. See Full, a., and cf. Più, Pleonasm.

plush.etymology: F. pluche, peluche (cf. It. peluzzo), fr. L. pilus hair. See pile hair, and cf. Peruke.

pluviometer.etymology: L. pluvia rain + -meter: cf. F. pluviomètre.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

ply.etymology: OE. plien, F. plier to fold, to bend, fr. L. plicare; akin to Gr. flechten. Cf. Apply, Complex, Display, Duplicity, Employ, Exploit, Implicate, Plait, Pliant, Flax.

pneumatic.etymology: L. pneumaticus, Gr. fnehan: cf. F. pneumatique. Cf. Pneumonia.

roots.meaning: A combining form from Gr. a lung; as, pneumogastric, pneumology.
A combining form from Gr. a lung; as, pneumogastric, pneumology.
A combining form from Gr. a lung; as, pneumogastric, pneumology.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

poach.etymology: F. pocher to place in a pocket, to poach eggs (the yolk of the egg being as it were pouched in the white), from poche pocket, pouch. See Pouch, v. &n.

pock.etymology: OE. pokke, AS. pocc, poc; akin to D. pok, G. pocke, and perh. to E. poke a pocket. Cf. Pox.

pocket.etymology: OE. poket, Prov. F. & OF. poquette, F. pochette, dim. fr. poque, pouque, F. poche; probably of Teutonic origin. See Poke a pocket, and cf. Poach to cook eggs, to plunder, and Pouch.

pod.etymology: Probably akin to pudding, and perhaps the same word as pad a cushion; cf. also Dan. pude pillow, cushion, and also E. cod a husk, pod.

podiceps.etymology: NL., fr. L. podex, podicis, anus + pes foot.

poesy.etymology: F. poésie (cf. It. poesia), L. poesis, from Gr. Posy.

poet.etymology: F. poëte, L. poëta, fr. Gr. Poem.

poignant.etymology: F., p. pr. of poindre to sting, fr. L. pungere to prick, sting. See Pungent.

poinciana.etymology: NL. Named after M. de Poinci, a governor of the French West Indies.

poinsettia.etymology: NL. Named after Joel R. Poinsett of South Carolina.

point.etymology: F. point, and probably also pointe, L. punctum, puncta, fr. pungere, punctum, to prick. See Pungent, and cf. Puncto, Puncture.

poise.etymology: OE. pois, peis, OF. pois, peis, F. poids, fr. L. pensum a portion weighed out, pendere to weigh, weigh out. Cf. Avoirdupois, Pendant, Poise, v.

poison.etymology: F. poison, in Old French also, a potion, fr. L. potio a drink, draught, potion, a poisonous draught, fr. potare to drink. See Potable, and cf. Potion.

poke.etymology: AS. poca, poha, pohha; akin to Icel. poki, OD. poke, and perh. to E. pock; cf. also Gael.poca, and OF. poque. Cf. Pock, Pocket, Pouch.

polar.etymology: Cf. F. polaire. See Pole of the earth.

pole.etymology: Cf. G. Pole a Pole, Polen Poland.

poleax.etymology: OE. pollax; cf. OD. pollexe. See Poll head, and Ax.

poleaxe.etymology: OE. pollax; cf. OD. pollexe. See Poll head, and Ax.

polecat.etymology: Probably fr. F. poule hen, and originally, a poultry cat, because it feeds on poultry. See Poultry.

polenta.etymology: It., fr. L. polenta peeled barley.

police.etymology: F., fr. L. politia the condition of a state, government, administration, Gr. pur, puri. Cf. Policy polity, Polity.

policy.etymology: L. politia, Gr. police, Of. police. See Police, n.

polite.etymology: L. politus, p. p. of polire to polish: cf. F. poli. See Polish, v.

politic.etymology: L. politicus political, Gr. politique. See Police, and cf. ePolitical.

polity.etymology: L. politia, Gr. politie. See 1st Policy, Police.

polka.etymology: Pol. Polka a Polish woman: cf. F. & G. polka.

pollack.etymology: Cf. G. & D. pollack, and Gael. pollag a little pool, a sort of fish.

polliwog.etymology: OE. polwigle. Cf. Poll head, and Wiggle.

pollute.etymology: L. pollutus, p. p. of polluere to defile, to pollute, from a prep. appearing only in comp. + luere to wash. See Position, Lave.

pollux.etymology: L., the twin brother of castor; also, the constellation.

polo.etymology: Of Eastern origin; -- properly, the ball used in the game.

poltroon.etymology: F. poltron, from It. poltrone an idle fellow, sluggard, coward, poltro idle, lazy, also, bed, fr. OHG. polstar, bolstar, cushion, G. polster, akin to E. bolster. See Bolster.

polynomial.etymology: Poly- + -nomial, as in monomial, binomial: cf. F. polynôme.

pomade.etymology: F. pommade pomatum, OF. pomade cider (cf. Sp. pomada, It. pomata, LL. pomata a drink made of apples), from L. pomum fruit, LL., an apple. Cf. Pomatum.

pome.etymology: L. pomum a fruit: cf. F. pomme apple. Cf. Pomade.

pomegranate.etymology: OE. pomgarnet, OF. pome de grenate, F. grenade, L. pomum a fruit + granatus grained, having many grains or seeds. See Pome, and Garnet, Grain.

pomfret.etymology: Perhaps corrupt. fr. Pg. pampano a kind of fish.

pommel.etymology: OE. pomel, OF. pomel, F. pommeau, LL. pomellus, fr. L. pomum fruit, LL. also, an apple. See Pome.

pomology.etymology: L. pomum fruit + -logy: cf. F. pomologie.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

pomp.etymology: OE. pompe, F. pompe, L. pompa, fr. Gr. Pump a shoe.

pompous.etymology: F. pompeux, L. pomposus. See Pomp.

pond.etymology: Probably originally, an inclosed body of water, and the same word as pound. See Pound an inclosure.

ponder.etymology: L. ponderare, fr. pondus, ponderis, a weight, fr. pendere to weigh: cf. F. pondérer. See Pendant, and cf. Pound a weight.

ponderous.etymology: L. ponderosus, from pondus, -eris, a weight: cf. F. pondéreux. See Ponder.

poniard.etymology: F. poignard (cf. It. pugnale, Sp. puñal), fr. L. pugio, -onis; probably akin to pugnus fist, or fr. pugnus fist, as held in the fist. See Pugnacious.

pontiff.etymology: F. pontife, L. pontifex, -ficis; pons, pontis, a bridge (perhaps originally, a way, path) + facere to make. Cf. Pontoon.

pontifical.etymology: L. pontificalis: cf. F. pontifical. See Pontiff.

pontificate.etymology: L. pontificatus: cf. F. pontificat. See Pontiff.

pontoon.etymology: F. ponton (cf. It. pontone), from L. ponto, - onis, fr. pons, pontis, a bridge, perhaps originally, a way, path: cf. Gr. path, pathi, panthan. Cf. Punt a boat.

pool.etymology: AS. pol; akin to LG. pool, pohl, D. poel, G. pfuhl; cf. Icel. pollr, also W. pwll, Gael. poll.

poor.etymology: OE. poure or povre, OF. povre, F. pauvre, L. pauper; the first syllable of which is probably akin to paucus few (see Paucity, Few), and the second to parare to prepare, procure. See Few, and cf. Parade, Pauper, Poverty.

pope.etymology: AS. papa, L. papa father, bishop. Cf. Papa, Papal.

popinjay.etymology: OE. popingay, papejay, OF. papegai, papegaut; cf. Pr. papagai, Sp. & Pg. papagayo, It. pappagallo, LGr. gallus cock, or the same word as E. jay, F. geai. Cf. Papagay.

poplar.etymology: OE. popler, OF. poplier, F. peuplier, fr. L. populus poplar.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

poppy.etymology: OE. popy, AS. popig, L. papaver.

populace.etymology: F. populace, fr. It. popolaccio, popolazzo, fr. popolo people, L. populus. See People.

popular.etymology: L. popularis, fr. populus people: cf. F. populaire. See People.

popularity.etymology: L. popularitas an effort to please the people: cf. F. popularité.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix denoting an agent, or doer, one who practices, a believer in; as, theorist, one who theorizes; socialist, one who holds to socialism; sensualist, one given to sensuality.

populous.etymology: L. populosus, fr. populus people: cf. F. populeux.

porcelain.etymology: F. porcelaine, It. porcellana, orig., the porcelain shell, or Venus shell (Cypræa porcellana), from a dim. fr. L. porcus pig, probably from the resemblance of the shell in shape to a pig's back. Porcelain was called after this shell, either on account of its smoothness and whiteness, or because it was believed to be made from it. See Pork.

porch.etymology: F. porche, L. porticus, fr. porta a gate, entrance, or passage. See Port a gate, and cf. Portico.

porcine.etymology: L. porcinus, from porcus a swine. See Pork.

porcupine.etymology: OE. porkepyn, porpentine, OF. porc-espi, F. porc-épic (cf. It. porco spino, porco spinoso, Sp. puerco espino, puerco espin, fr. L. porcus swine + spina thorn, spine). The last part of the French word is perhaps a corruption from the It. or Sp.; cf. F. épi ear, a spike of grain, L. spica. See Pork, Spike a large nail, Spine.

pore.etymology: F., fr. L. porus, Gr. Fare, v.

porifera.etymology: NL., fr. L. porus pore + ferre to bear.

pork.etymology: F. porc, L. porcus hog, pig. See Farrow a litter of pigs, and cf. Porcelain, Porpoise.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

porous.etymology: Cf. F. poreux. See Pore, n.

porphyry.etymology: F. porphyre, L. porphyrites, fr. Gr. Purple.

porpoise.etymology: OE. porpeys, OF. porpeis, literally, hog fish, from L. porcus swine + piscis fish. See Pork, and Fish.

porridge.etymology: Probably corrupted fr. pottage; perh. influenced by OE. porree a kind of pottage, OF. porrée, fr. L. porrum, porrus, leek. See Pottage, and cf. Porringer.

porringer.etymology: OE. pottanger, for pottager; cf. F. potager a soup basin. See Porridge.

port.etymology: From Oporto, in Portugal, i. e., the port, L. portus. See Port harbor.

porta.etymology: L., a gate. See Port a hole.

portable.etymology: L. portabilis, fr. portare to carry: cf. F. portable. See Port demeanor.

portal.etymology: OF. portal, F. portail, LL. portale, fr. L. porta a gate. See Port a gate.

portcullis.etymology: OF. porte coulisse, coleïce, a sliding door, fr. L. colare, colatum, to filter, to strain: cf. F. couler to glide. See Port a gate, and cf. Cullis, Colander.

porte.etymology: F. porte a gate, L. porta. See Port a gate.

portend.etymology: L. portendre, portentum, to foretell, to predict, to impend, from an old preposition used in comp. + tendere to stretch. See Position, Tend.

porter.etymology: F. portier, L. portarius, from porta a gate, door. See Port a gate.

portfolio.etymology: F. portefeuille; porter to carry + feuille a leaf. See Port to carry, and Folio.

portiere.etymology: F., fr. porte gate, door. See Port a gate.

portion.etymology: F., from L. portio, akin to pars, partis, a part. See Part, n.

portmanteau.etymology: F. porte-manteau; porter to carry + manteau a cloak, mantle. See Port to carry, and Mantle.

portrait.etymology: F., originally p. p. of portraire to portray. See Portray.

portray.etymology: OE. pourtraien, OF. portraire, pourtraire, F. portraire, fr. L. protrahere, protractum, to draw or drag forth; pro forward, forth + trahere to draw. See Trace, v. t., and cf. Protract.

portuguese.etymology: Cf. F. portugais, Sp. portugues, Pg. portuguez.

posit.etymology: L. ponere, positum, to place. See Position.

position.etymology: F. position, L. positio, fr. ponere, positum, to put, place; prob. for posino, fr. an old preposition used only in comp. (akin to Gr. sinere to leave, let, permit, place. See Site, and cf. Composite, Compound, v., Depone, Deposit, Expound, Impostor, Opposite, Propound, Pose, v., Posit, Post, n.

positive.etymology: OE. positif, F. positif, L. positivus. See Position.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

possess.etymology: L. possessus, p. p. of possidere to have, possess, from an inseparable prep. (cf. Position) + sedere to sit. See Sit.

possible.etymology: F., fr. L. possibilis, fr. posse to be able, to have power; potis able, capable + esse to be. See Potent, Am, and cf. Host a landlord.

post.etymology: F. aposter to place in a post or position, generally for a bad purpose.

postcava.etymology: NL. See Post-, and Cave, n.

posterior.etymology: L. posterior, compar. of posterus coming after, from post after. See Post-.

posterity.etymology: L. posteritas: cf. F. postérité. See Posterior.

postern.etymology: OF. posterne, posterle, F. poterne, fr. L. posterula, fr. posterus coming after. See Posterior.

postfix.etymology: Pref. post- + -fix, as in prefix: cf. F. postfixe.

posthumous.etymology: L. posthumus, postumus, properly, last; hence, late born (applied to children born after the father's death, or after he had made his will), superl. of posterus, posterior. See Posterior.

postilion.etymology: F. postillon, It. postiglione, fr. posta post. See Post a postman.

postmeridian.etymology: L. postmeridianus; post after + meridianus. See Meridian.

postpone.etymology: L. postponere, postpositum; post after + ponere to place, put. See Post-, and Position.

postpose.etymology: F. postposer. See Post-, and Pose, v. t.
