postscript.etymology: L. postscriptus, (assumed) p. p. of postscribere to write after; post after + scribere to write: cf. F. postscriptum. See Post-, and Scribe.

postulant.etymology: F., fr. L. postulans, p. pr. of postulare. See Postulate.

postulate.etymology: L. postulatum a demand, request, prop. p. p. of postulare to demand, prob. a dim. of poscere to demand, prob. for porcscere; akin to G. forschen to search, investigate, Skr. prach to ask, and L. precari to pray: cf. F. postulat. See Pray.

posture.etymology: F., fr. L. positura, fr. ponere, positum, to place. See Position.

pot.etymology: Akin to LG. pott, D. pot, Dan. potte, Sw. potta, Icel. pottr, F. pot; of unknown origin.

potable.etymology: F., fr. L. potabilis, fr. potare to drink; akin to Gr. po`tos a drinking, po`sis a drink, Skr. pa to drink, OIr. ibim I drink. Cf. Poison, Bib, Imbibe.

potation.etymology: L. potatio, fr. potare. See Potable.

potato.etymology: Sp. patata potato, batata sweet potato, from the native American name (probably batata) in Hayti.

poteen.etymology: Cf. Ir. potaim, poitim, I drink, poitin a small pot.

potence.etymology: F., fr. LL. potentia staff, crutch, L., might, power. See Potency.

potency.etymology: L. potentia, from potens, -entis, potent. See Potent, and cf. Potance, Potence, Puissance.

potent.etymology: L. potens, -entis, p. pr. of posse to be able, to have power, fr. potis able, capable (akin to Skr. pati master, lord) + esse to be. See Host a landlord, Am, and cf. Despot, Podesta, Possible, Power, Puissant.

potentate.etymology: LL. potentatus, fr. potentare to exercise power: cf. F. potentat. See Potent, a.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

pother.etymology: Cf. D. peuteren to rummage, poke. Cf. Potter, Pudder.

potion.etymology: L. potio, from potare to drink: cf. F. potion. See Poison.

potpourri.etymology: F., fr. pot pot + pourri, p. p. of pourrir to rot, L. putrere. Cf. Olla-podrida.

pottage.etymology: F. potage, fr. pot pot. See Pot, and cf. Porridge, Porringer.

pottery.etymology: F. poterie, fr. pot. See Pot.

pottle.etymology: OE. potel, OF. potel, dim. of pot. See Pot.

pouch.etymology: F. poche a pocket, pouch, bag; probably of Teutonic origin. See Poke a bag, and cf. Poach to cook eggs, to plunder.

poultice.etymology: L. puls, pl. pultes, a thick pap; akin to Gr. po`ltos. Cf. Pulse seeds.

pounce.etymology: F. ponce pumice, pounce, fr. L. pumex, -icis, pumice. See Pumice.

pound.etymology: OE. pounen, AS. punian to bruise. Cf. Pun a play on words.

pour.etymology: OE. pouren, of uncertain origin; cf. W. bwrw to cast, throw, shed, bwrw gwlaw to rain.

poverty.etymology: OE. poverte, OF. poverté, F. pauvreté, fr. L. paupertas, fr. pauper poor. See Poor.

powder.etymology: OE. poudre, pouldre, F. poudre, OF. also poldre, puldre, L. pulvis, pulveris: cf. pollen fine flour, mill dust, E. pollen. Cf. Polverine, Pulverize.

power.etymology: OE. pouer, poer, OF. poeir, pooir, F. pouvoir, n. & v., fr. LL. potere, for L. posse, potesse, to be able, to have power. See Possible, Potent, and cf. Posse comitatus.

pox.etymology: For pocks, OE. pokkes. See Pock. It is plural in form but is used as a singular.

practicable.etymology: LL. practicare to act, transact, fr. L. practicus active, Gr. practicable, pratiquer to practice. See Practical.

practical.etymology: L. practicus active, Gr. pratique, formerly also practique. Cf. Pragmatic, Practice.

practice.etymology: OE. praktike, practique, F. pratique, formerly also, practique, LL. practica, fr. Gr. Practical, and cf. Pratique, Pretty.

praenomen.etymology: L., fr. prae before + nomen name.

pragmatic.etymology: L. pragmaticus busy, active, skilled in business, especially in law and state affairs, systematic, Gr. pragmatique. See Practical.

pragmatical.etymology: L. pragmaticus busy, active, skilled in business, especially in law and state affairs, systematic, Gr. pragmatique. See Practical.

prairie.etymology: F., an extensive meadow, OF. praerie, LL. prataria, fr. L. pratum a meadow.

praise.etymology: OE. preisen, OF. preisier, prisier, F. priser, L. pretiare to prize, fr. pretium price. See Price, n., and cf. Appreciate, Praise, n., Prize, v.

prakrit.etymology: Skr. prakrsta original, natural, usual, common, vulgar.

prance.etymology: OE. prauncen; probably akin to prank, v. t. See Prank.

prank.etymology: Cf. E. prink, also G. prangen, prunken, to shine, to make a show, Dan. prange, prunke, Sw. prunka, D. pronken.

roots.meaning: A combining form signifying green; as, praseocobalt, a green variety of cobalt.

prate.etymology: Akin to LG. & D. praten, Dan. prate, Sw. & Icel. prata.

prawn.etymology: OE. prane, of unknown origin; cf. L. perna a sea mussel.

pray.etymology: OE. preien, OF. preier, F. prier, L. precari, fr. prex, precis, a prayer, a request; akin to Skr. prach to ask, AS. frignan, frinan, fricgan, G. fragen, Goth. fraíhnan. Cf. Deprecate, Imprecate, Precarious.

prayer.etymology: OE. preiere, OF. preiere, F. prière, fr. L. precarius obtained by prayer, fr. precari to pray. See Pray, v. i.

preach.etymology: OE. prechen, OF. preechier, F. prêcher, fr. L. praedicare to cry in public, to proclaim; prae before + dicare to make known, dicere to say; or perhaps from (assumed) LL. praedictare. See Diction, and cf. Predicate, Predict.

preacher.etymology: Cf. OF. preeschierre, prescheur, F. prêcheur, L. praedicator.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

preamble.etymology: LL. praeambulum, from L. praeambulus walking before, fr. praeambulare to walk before; prae before + ambulare to walk: cf. F. préambule. See Amble.

prebend.etymology: F. prébende (cf. It. & Sp. prebenda), from L. praebenda, from L. praebere to hold forth, afford, contr. fr. praehibere; prae before + habere to have, hold. See Habit, and cf. Provender.

prebendary.etymology: LL. praebendarius: cf. F. prébendaire. See Prebend.

precarious.etymology: L. precarius obtained by begging or prayer, depending on request or on the will of another, fr. precari to pray, beg. See Pray.

precative.etymology: L. precativus, precatorius, fr. precari to pray. See Precarious.

precatory.etymology: L. precativus, precatorius, fr. precari to pray. See Precarious.

precaution.etymology: F. précation, L. praecautio, fr. praecavere, praecautum, to guard against beforehand; prae before + cavere be on one's guard. See Pre-, and Caution.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

precede.etymology: L. praecedere, praecessum; prae before + cedere to go, to be in motion: cf. F. préceder. See Pre-, and Cede.

precedent.etymology: L. praecedens, -entis, p. pr. of praecedere: cf. F. précédent. See Precede.

precentor.etymology: L. praecentor, fr. praecinere to sing before; prae before + canere to sing. See Chant.

precept.etymology: L. praeceptum, from praecipere to take beforehand, to instruct, teach; prae before + capere to take: cf. F. précepte. See Pre-, and Capacious.

preceptor.etymology: L. praeceptor, fr. praecipere to teach: cf. F. précepteur. See Precept.

precession.etymology: L. praecedere, praecessum, to go before: cf. F. précession. See Precede.

precinct.etymology: LL. praecinctum, fr. L. praecingere, praecinctum, to gird about, to encompass; prae before + cingere to gird, surround. See Pre-, and Cincture.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

precious.etymology: OF. precious, precius, precios, F. précieux, L. pretiosus, fr. pretium price, worth, value. See Price.

precipice.etymology: F. précipice, L. praecipitium, fr. praeceps, - cipitis, headlong; prae before + caput, capitis, the head. See Pre-, and Chief.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

precipitant.etymology: L. praecipitans, -antis, p. pr. of praecipitare: cf. F. précipitant. See Precipitate.

precipitate.etymology: L. praecipitatus, p. p. of praecipitare to precipitate, fr. praeceps headlong. See Precipice.

precipitous.etymology: L. praeceps, -cipitis: cf. OF. precipiteux. See Precipice.

precise.etymology: L. praecisus cut off, brief, concise, p. p. of praecidere to cut off in front, to cut off; prae before + caedere to cut: cf. F. précis. Cf. Concise.

precision.etymology: Cf. F. précision, L. praecisio a cutting off. See Precise.

preclude.etymology: L. praecludere, praeclusum; prae before + claudere to shut. See Close, v.

precocious.etymology: L. praecox, -ocis, and praecoquus, fr. praecoquere to cook or ripen beforehand; prae before + coquere to cook. See 3d Cook, and cf. Apricot.

precognition.etymology: L. praecognitio, fr. praecognoscere to foreknow. See Pre-, and Cognition.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

precordial.etymology: Pref. pre- + L. cor, cordis, heart: cf. F. précordial.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

precursor.etymology: L. praecursor, fr. praecurrere to run before; prae before + currere to run. See Course.

predation.etymology: L. praedatio, fr. praedari to plunder.

predatory.etymology: L. praedatorius, fr. praedari to plunder, fr. praeda prey. See Prey.

predecessor.etymology: L. praedecessor; prae before + decessor one who withdraws from the province he has governed, a retiring officer (with reference to his successor), a predecessor, fr. decedere: cf. F. prédécesseur. See Decease.

predestinate.etymology: L. praedestinatus, p. p. of praedestinare to predestine; prae before + destinare to determine. See Destine.

predetermine.etymology: Pref. pre- + determine: cf. F. prédéterminer.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

predicament.etymology: Cf. F. prédicament, L. praedicamentum. See Predicate.

predicate.etymology: L. praedicatus, p. p. of praedicare to cry in public, to proclaim. See Preach.

predict.etymology: L. praedictus, p. p. of praedicere to predict; prae before + dicere to say, tell. See Diction, and cf. Preach.

predilection.etymology: Pref. pre- + L. dilectus, p. p. diligere to prefer: cf. F. prédilection. See Diligent.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

predispose.etymology: Pref. pre- + dispose: cf. F. prédisposer.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

predisposition.etymology: Pref. pre- + disposition: cf. F. prédisposition.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

predominate.etymology: Pref. pre- + dominate: cf. F. prédominer.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

preeminence.etymology: F. pré\'82minence, L. praeeminentia. See Preëminent.

preeminent.etymology: L. praeminens, -entis, p. pr. praeminere to be prominent, to surpass: cf. F. pré\'82minent. See Pre-, and Eminent.

preemption.etymology: Pref. pre- + emption: cf. F. préemption. See Redeem.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

preen.etymology: AS. preón a clasp, bodkin; akin to D. priem punch, bodkin, awl, G. pfriem, Icel. prjonn a knitting needle, pin, Dan. preen a bodkin, punch.

preface.etymology: F. préface; cf. Sp. prefacio, prefacion, It. prefazio, prefazione; all fr. L. praefatio, fr. praefari to speak or say beforehand; prae before + fari, fatus, to speak. See Fate.

prefect.etymology: L. praefectus, fr. praefectus, p. p. of praeficere to set over; prae before + facere to make: cf. F. préfet.

prefer.etymology: F. préférer, L. praeferre; prae before + ferre to bear or carry. See 1st Bear.

prefigure.etymology: F. préfigurer, or L. praefigurare, praefiguratum; prae before + figurare to figure. See Figure, and cf. Prefigurate.

prefix.etymology: L. praefixus, p. p. of praefigere to fix or fasten before; prae before + figere to fix: cf. F. préfix fixed beforehand, determined, préfixer to prefix. See Fix.

preform.etymology: L. praeformare. See Pre-, and Form.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

pregnant.etymology: L. praegnans, -antis; prae before + genere, gignere, to beget: cf. F. prégnant. See Gender, 2d Kin.

prehensile.etymology: L. prehensus, p. p. of prehendere to lay hold of, seize; pre- (equiv. to prae before) + hendere (in comp.), akin to E. get: cf. F. préhensile. See Get, and cf. Prison, Prize, n.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

prehension.etymology: L. prehensio; cf. F. préhension. See Prehensile.

prejudge.etymology: Pref. pre + judge: cf. F. préjuger. Cf. Prejudicate, Prejudice.

prejudice.etymology: F. préjudice, L. praejudicium; prae before + judicium judgment. See Prejudicate, Judicial.

prejudicial.etymology: L. praejudicialis belonging to a preceding judgment: cf. F. préjudiciel.

prelacy.etymology: LL. praelatia. See Prelate; cf. Prelaty.

prelate.etymology: F. prélat, LL. praelatus, fr. L. praelatus, used as p. p. of praeferre to prefer, but from a different root. See Elate.

preliminary.etymology: Pref. pre + L. liminaris belonging to a threshold, fr. limen, liminis, threshold, entrance: cf. F. préliminaire. Cf. Limit.

prelude.etymology: F. prélude (cf. It. preludio, LL. praeludium), fr. L. prae before + ludus play. See Prelude, v. t.

premature.etymology: L. praematurus; prae before + maturus ripe. See Mature.

premeditate.etymology: L. praemeditatus, p. p. of praemeditari; prae before + meditari to meditate. See Meditate.

premier.etymology: F. premier, fr. L. primarius of the first rank, principal, fr. primus the first. See Primary, Prime, a.

premiere.etymology: F., prop. fem. of premier first. See Premier, a.

premise.etymology: F. prémisse, fr. L. praemissus, p. p. of praemittere to send before; prae before + mittere to send. See Mission.

premium.etymology: L. praemium, originally, what one has got before or better than others; prae before + emere to take, buy. See Redeem.

preoccupy.etymology: Cf. F. préoccuper. See Preoccupate, Occupy.

preordain.etymology: Pref. pre + ordain: cf. L. praeordinare.

preparation.etymology: F. préparation, L. praeparatio. See Prepare.

prepare.etymology: F. préparer, L. praeparare; prae before + parare to make ready. See Pare.

preponderant.etymology: L. praeponderans, -antis: cf. F. prépondérant. See Preponderate.

preponderate.etymology: L. praeponderatus, p. p. of praeponderare; prae before + ponderare to weigh, fr., pondus, ponderis, a weight. See Ponder.

prepose.etymology: F. préposer; pref. pré- (L. prae before) + poser. See Pose.

preposition.etymology: L. praepositio, fr. praeponere to place before; prae before + ponere to put, place: cf. F. préposition. See Position, and cf. Provost.

preposterous.etymology: L. praeposterus; prae before + posterus coming after, latter. See Posterior.

prerogative.etymology: F. prérogative, from L. praerogativa precedence in voting, preference, privilege, fr. praerogativus that is asked before others for his opinion, that votes before or first, fr. praerogare to ask before another; prae before + rogare to ask. See Rogation.

presage.etymology: F. présage, L. praesagium, from praesagire. See Presage, v. t.

presbyter.etymology: L. an elder, fr. Gr. Priest.

presbytery.etymology: L. presbyterium, Gr. Presbyter, and cf. Presbyterium.

prescience.etymology: F. prescience, L. praescientia. See Prescient.

prescient.etymology: L. praesciens, -entis, p. pr. of praescire to foreknow; prae before + scire to know: cf. F. prescient. See Science.

prescribe.etymology: L. praescribere, praescriptum; prae before + scriebe to write. See Scribe.

prescript.etymology: L. praescriptus, p. p. of praescribere: cf. F. prescrit. See Prescribe.

prescription.etymology: F. prescription, L. praescriptio,an inscription, preface, precept, demurrer, prescription (in sense 3), fr. praescribere. See Prescribe.

prescriptive.etymology: L. praescriptivus of a demurrer or legal exception.

presence.etymology: F. présence, L. praesentia. See Present.

present.etymology: F. présent, L. praesens,-entis, that is before one, in sight or at hand, p. p. of praeesse to be before; prae before + esse to be. See Essence.

presentation.etymology: L. praesentatio a showing, representation: cf. F. présentation.

presentiment.etymology: Pref. pre- + sentiment: cf. F. pressentiment. See Presentient.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

preserve.etymology: F. préserver, from L. prae before + servare to save, preserve; cf. L. praeservare to observe beforehand. See Serve.

preside.etymology: L. praesidere; prae before + sedere to sit: cf. F. présider. See Sit.

president.etymology: F. président, L. praesidens, -entis, p. pr. of praesidere. See Preside.

press.etymology: Corrupt. fr. prest ready money advanced, a loan; hence, earnest money given soldiers on entering service. See Prest, n.

pressure.etymology: OF., fr. L. pressura, fr. premere. See 4th Press.

prestidigitator.etymology: L. praesto ready + digitus finger: cf. F. prestidigitateur.

prestige.etymology: F., fr. L. praestigum delusion, illusion, praestigae deceptions, jugglers' tricks, prob. fr. prae before + the root of stinguere to extinguish, originally, to prick. See Stick, v.

presto.etymology: It. or Sp. presto quick, quickly. See Prest, a.

presume.etymology: F. présumer, L. praesumere, praesumptum; prae before + sumere to take. See Assume, Redeem.

presumption.etymology: L. praesumptio: cf. F. présomption, OF. also presumpcion. See Presume.

presumptuous.etymology: L. praesumptuosus: cf. F. présomptueux, OF. also presumptuous. See Presumption.

presuppose.etymology: Pref. pre- + suppose: cf. F. présupposer.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

presupposition.etymology: Pref. pre- + supposition: cf. F. présupposition.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

pretence.etymology: LL. praetensus, for L. praetentus, p. p. of praetendere. See Pretend, and cf. Tension.

pretend.etymology: OE. pretenden to lay claim to, F. prétendre, L. praetendere, praetentum, to stretch forward, pretend, simulate, assert; prae before + tendere to stretch. See Tend, v. t.

pretense.etymology: LL. praetensus, for L. praetentus, p. p. of praetendere. See Pretend, and cf. Tension.

pretension.etymology: Cf. F. prétention. See Pretend, Tension.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying past, by, beyond, more than; as, preter- mission, a permitting to go by; preternatural, beyond or more than is natural. [Written also præter.]
A noun suffix denoting an agent, or doer, one who practices, a believer in; as, theorist, one who theorizes; socialist, one who holds to socialism; sensualist, one given to sensuality.

preterit.etymology: L. praeteritus, p. p. of praeterire to go or pass by; praeter beyond, by + ire to go: cf. F. prétérit. See Issue.

pretermit.etymology: L. praetermittere, praetermissum; praeter beyond + mittere to send. See Mission.

pretext.etymology: F. prétexte, L. praetextum, fr. praetextus, p. p. of praetexere to weave before, allege as an excuse; prae before + texere to weave. See Text.

pretor.etymology: L. praetor, for praeitor, fr. praeire to go before; prae before + ire to go. See Issue.

pretty.etymology: OE. prati, AS. prættig, prætig, crafty, sly, akin to præt, prætt, deceit, trickery, Icel. prettugr tricky, prettr a trick; probably fr. Latin, perhaps through Celtic; cf. W. praith act, deed, practice, LL. practica execution, practice, plot. See Practice.

prevail.etymology: F. prévaloir, OF. prevaleir, L. praevalere; prae before + valere to be strong, able, or worth. See Valiant.

prevalence.etymology: L. praevalentia: cf. F. prévalence. See Prevail.

prevalent.etymology: L. praevalens, -entis, p. pr. of praevalere. See Prevail.

prevaricate.etymology: L. praevaricatus, p. p. of praevaricari to walk crookedly, to collude; prae before + varicare to straddle, fr. varicus straddling, varus bent. See Varicose.

prevent.etymology: L. praevenire, praeventum; prae before + venire to come. See Come.

previous.etymology: L. praevius going before, leading the way; prae before + via the way. See Voyage.

previse.etymology: L. praevisus, p. p. of praevidere to foresee; prae before + videre to see. See Vision.

prey.etymology: OF. preie, F. proie, L. praeda, probably for praeheda. See Prehensile, and cf. Depredate, Predatory.

priapism.etymology: L. priapismus, Gr. Priapus the god of procreation, the penis, Gr. priapisme.

price.etymology: OE. pris, OF. pris, F. prix, L. pretium; cf. Gr. pa to buy, OI. renim I sell. Cf. Appreciate, Depreciate, Interpret, Praise, n. & v., Precious, Prize.

prick.etymology: AS. prica, pricca, pricu; akin to LG. prick, pricke, D. prik, Dan. prik, prikke, Sw. prick. Cf. Prick, v.

pricket.etymology: Perhaps so called from the state of his horns. See Prick, and cf. Brocket.

prickle.etymology: AS. pricele, pricle; akin to LG. prickel, D. prikkel. See Prick, n.

pride.etymology: Cf. AS. lamprede, LL. lampreda, E. lamprey.

priest.etymology: OE. prest, preost, AS. preóst, fr. L. presbyter, Gr. pristinus. Cf. Pristine, Presbyter.

primacy.etymology: LL. primatia, fr. L. primas, -atis, one of the first or principal, chief, fr. primus first: cf. F. primatie. See Prime, a.

primal.etymology: LL. primalis, fr. L. primus the first. See Prime, a.

primary.etymology: L. primarius, fr. primus first: cf. F. primaire. See Prime, a., and cf. Premier, Primero.

primate.etymology: OE. primat, F. primat, L. primas, -atis one of the first, chief, fr. primus the first. See Prime, a.

prime.etymology: F., fr. L. primus first, a superl. corresponding to the compar. prior former. See Prior, a., Foremost, Former, and cf. Prim, a., Primary, Prince.

primer.etymology: OF. primer, primier, premier, F. premier. See Premier.

primeval.etymology: L. primaevus; primus first + aevum age. See Prime, a., and Age.

primipara.etymology: L., fr. primus first + parere to bring forth.

primitive.etymology: L. primitivus, fr. primus the first: cf. F. primitif. See Prime, a.

primogenitor.etymology: LL., fr. L. primus first + genitor a begetter.

primogeniture.etymology: LL., fr. L. primus first + genitura a begetting, birth, generation, fr. genere, gignere, to beget: cf. F. primogéniture, L. primogenitus firstborn. See Prime, a., and Genus, Kin.

primordial.etymology: L. primordialis, from primordium the first beginning; primus first + ordiri to begin a web, to begin: cf. F. primordial.

primrose.etymology: OE. primerole, F. primerole, a derivative fr. LL. primula, from L. primus first. See Prime, a.

prince.etymology: F., from L. princeps, -cipis, the first, chief; primus first + capere to take. See Prime, a., and Capacious.

princess.etymology: F. princesse. See Prince, and cf. Princesse.

principal.etymology: F., from L. principalis. See Prince.

principality.etymology: L. principalitas preëminence, excellence: cf. F. principalité, principauté. See Principal.

principle.etymology: F. principe, L. principium beginning, foundation, fr. princeps, -cipis. See Prince.

prink.etymology: Probably a nasalized form of prick. See Prick, v. t., and cf. Prig, Prank.

print.etymology: Abbrev. fr. imprint. See Imprint, and Press to squeeze.

prior.etymology: L. prior former, previous, better, superior; compar. corresponding to primus first, and pro for. See Former, and cf. Prime, a., and Pre-, Pro-.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting priority (of time, place, or rank); as, precede, to go before; precursor, a forerunner; prefix, to fix or place before; preëminent eminent before or above others. Pre- is sometimes used intensively, as in prepotent, very potent. [Written also præ-.]

A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of, in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, to go before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, part spoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to look out for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a person acting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according to parts.

priority.etymology: Cf. F. priorité. See Prior, a.

priory.etymology: Cf. LL. prioria. See Prior, n.

prison.etymology: F., fr. L. prehensio, prensio, a seizing, arresting, fr. prehendre, prendere, to lay hold of, to seize. See Prehensile, and cf. Prize, n., Misprision.

pristine.etymology: L. pristinus, akin to prior: cf. F. pristin. See Prior, a.

private.etymology: L. privatus apart from the state, peculiar to an individual, private, properly p. p. of privare to bereave, deprive, originally, to separate, fr. privus single, private, perhaps originally, put forward (hence, alone, single) and akin to prae before. See Prior, a., and cf. Deprive, Privy, a.

privation.etymology: L. privatio: cf. F. privation. See Private.

privet.etymology: Cf. Scot. privie, Prov. E. prim-print, primwort. Prob. for primet, and perh. named from being cut and trimmed. See, Prim, a., and cf. Prime to prune, Prim, n., Prie, n.

privilege.etymology: From Middle English privilege , from Anglo-Norman privilege and Old French privilege , from Latin prīvilēgium ( “ ordinance or law against or in favor of an individual ” ) , from prīvus ( “ private ” ) + lēx, lēg- ( “ law ” ) . Displaced native Old English frēols ( “ privilege, immunity ” ) .

privy.etymology: F. privé, fr. L. privatus. See Private.

prize.etymology: F. prise a seizing, hold, grasp, fr. pris, p. p. of prendre to take, L. prendere, prehendere; in some senses, as 2 (b), either from, or influenced by, F. prix price. See Prison, Prehensile, and cf. Pry, and also Price.

pro.etymology: L.; akin to prae before, Gr. for. See For, prep., and cf. Prior, a.

probable.etymology: L. probabilis, fr. probare to try, approve, prove: cf. F. probable. See Prove, and cf. Provable.

probate.etymology: From L. probatus, p. p. of probare to prove. See Prove.

probation.etymology: L. probatio, fr. probare to try, examine, prove: cf. F. probation. See Prove.

probe.etymology: L. probare to try, examine. See Prove.

probity.etymology: F. probité, fr. L. probitas, fr. probus good, proper, honest. Cf. Prove.

problem.etymology: F. problème, L. problema, fr. Gr. Parable.

proceed.etymology: F. procéder. fr. L. procedere, processum, to go before, to proceed; pro forward + cedere to move. See Cede.

process.etymology: F. procès, L. processus. See Proceed.

procession.etymology: F., fr. L. processio. See Proceed.

proclaim.etymology: OE. proclamen, L. proclamare; pro before, forward + clamare to call or cry out: cf. F. proclamer. See Claim.

proclamation.etymology: F. proclamation, L. proclamatio. See Proclaim.

proconsul.etymology: L., fr. pro for + consul consul.

procrastinate.etymology: L. procrastinatus, p. p. of procrastinare to procrastinate; pro forward + crastinus of to-morrow, fr. cras to- morrow.

roots.meaning: An obsolete intensive prefix used in the formation of compound verbs; as in to-beat, to-break, to-hew, to-rend, to-tear. See these words in the Vocabulary. See the Note on All to, or All-to, under All, adv.

procreate.etymology: L. procreatus, p. p. of procreare; pro forward, forth + create to create.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

proctor.etymology: OE. proketour, contr. fr. procurator. See Procurator.

procumbent.etymology: L. procumbens, -entis, p. pr. of procumbere to fall, bend, or lean forward; pro forward + cumbere (in comp.), akin to cubare to lie down: cf. F. procombant. Cf. Incumbent.

procurator.etymology: L.: cf. F. procurateur. See Procure, and cf. Proctor.

procure.etymology: F. procurer, L. procurare, procuratum, to take care of; pro for + curare to take care, fr. cura care. See Cure, and cf. Proctor, Proxy.

prod.etymology: Cf. Gael. & Ir. brod goad, prickle, sting, and E. brad, also W. procio to poke, thrust.

prodigal.etymology: L. prodigus, from prodigere to drive forth, to squander away; pro forward, forth + agere to drive; cf. F. prodigue. See Agent.

prodigality.etymology: F. prodigalité, L. prodigalitas. See Prodigal.

prodigious.etymology: L. prodigiosus, fr. prodigium a prodigy; cf. F. prodigieux. See Prodigy.

prodigy.etymology: L. prodigium; pro before + (perh.) a word appearing in adagium adage: cf. F. prodige. Cf. Adage.

produce.etymology: L. producere, productum, to bring forward, beget, produce; pro forward, forth + ducere to lead. See Duke.

product.etymology: L. productus, p. pr. of producere. See Produce.

production.etymology: L. productio a lengthening, prolonging: cf. F. production. See Produce.

productive.etymology: F. productif, L. productivus fit for prolongation.

profanation.etymology: L. profanatio: cf. F. profanation. See Profane, v. t.

profane.etymology: F., fr. L. profanus, properly, before the temple, i. e., without the temple, unholy; pro before + fanum temple. See 1st Fane.

profess.etymology: F. profès, masc., professe, fem., professed (monk or nun), L. professus, p. p. of profiteri to profess; pro before, forward + fateri to confess, own. See Confess.

profession.etymology: F., fr. L. professio. See Profess, v.

professor.etymology: L., a teacher, a public teacher: cf. F. professeur. See Profess.

proffer.etymology: OE. profren, proferen, F. proférer, fr. L. proferre to bring forth or forward, to offer; pro forward + ferre to bring. See Bear to produce.

profile.etymology: It. profilo, fr. L. pro before + filum a thread, an outline, shape: cf. F. profil. See File arow, and cf. Purfle, Purl, a fringe.

profit.etymology: F., fr. L. profectus advance, progress, profit, fr. profectum. See Proficient.

profligate.etymology: L. profligatus, p. p. of profligare to strike or dash to the ground, to destroy; pro before + a word akin to fligere to strike. See Afflict.

profound.etymology: F. profond, L. profundus; pro before, forward + fundus the bottom. See Found to establish, Bottom lowest part.

profundity.etymology: L. profunditas: cf. F. profondite. See Profound.

profuse.etymology: L. profusus, p. p. of profundere to pour forth or out; pro forward, forth + fundere to pour: cf. F. profus. See Fuse to melt.

progenitor.etymology: OF. progeniteur, L. progenitor, fr. progignere, progenitum, to bring forth, to beget; pro forth + gignere to beget. See Gender kind.

progeny.etymology: OE. progenie, F. progénie, fr. L. progenies, fr. progignere. See Progenitor.

programme.etymology: L. programma a public proclamation, manifesto, Gr. programme. See Graphic.

progress.etymology: L. progressus, from progredi, p. p. progressus, to go forth or forward; pro forward + gradi to step, go: cf. F. progrès. See Grade.

prohibit.etymology: L. prohibitus, p. p. of prohibere to prohibit; pro before, forth + habere to have, hold. See Habit.

project.etymology: OF. project, F. projet, fr. L. projectus, p. p. of projicere to project; pro forward + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth, and cf. Projet.

prolapse.etymology: L. prolapsus, fr. prolapsus, p. p. of prolabi to fall forward; pro forward + labi to glide, fall.

prolate.etymology: L. prolatus, used as p. p. of proferre to bring forth, to extend; pro + latus, p. p. See Pro-, and Tolerate.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of, in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, to go before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, part spoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to look out for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a person acting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according to parts.

proliferate.etymology: L. proles offspring + ferre to bear.

prolific.etymology: F. prolifique, fr. L. proles offspring (from pro for, forward + the root of alere to nourish) + facere to make. See Adult, Old, and Fact.

prolix.etymology: L. prolixus extended, long, prolix, probably fr. pro before, forward + liqui to flow, akin to liquidus liquid; cf. OL. lixa water: cf. F. prolixe. See Liquid.

prologue.etymology: F., fr. L. prologus, fr. Gr. Logic.

prolong.etymology: F. prolonger, L. prolongare; pro before, forth + longus long. See Long, a., and cf. Prolongate, Purloin.

prolusion.etymology: L. prolusio, fr. proludere to prelude; pro before + ludere to play: cf. F. prolusion, It. prolusione.

promenade.etymology: F. (with a foreign suffix), from promener to lead, take for a walk, se promener to walk, from L. prominare to drive forward or along; pro forward + minare to drive animals. See Amenable, Menace.

prominence.etymology: L. prominentia: cf. F. prominence. See Prominent.

prominent.etymology: L. prominens, -entis, p. pr. of prominere to jut out, to project; pro before, forward + minere (in comp.) to jut, project: cf. F. prominent. See Imminent, Eminent.

promiscuous.etymology: L. promiscuus; pro before, in place of, for + miscere to mix. See Mix.

promise.etymology: F. promesse, L. promissum, fr. promittere, promissum, to put forth, foretell, promise; pro forward, for + mittere to send. See Mission.

promontory.etymology: L. promonturium, promunturium; pro before + mons, montis, mountain: cf. F. promontoire. See Mount, n.

promote.etymology: L. promotus, p. p. of promovere to move forward, to promote; pro forward + movere to move. See Move.

prompt.etymology: F. prompt, L. promptus, properly, brought forth (to light or view), hence, visible, evident, at hand, ready, quick, -- p. p. of promere to take or bring forth; pro forth + emere to take. See Redeem.

promptitude.etymology: F., fr. L. promptitudo. See Prompt, a.

promulgate.etymology: L. promulgatus, p. p. of promulgare to promulgate; of unknown origin. Cf. Promulge.

pronate.etymology: L. pronatus, p. p. of pronare to bend forward. See Prone.

prone.etymology: L. pronus, akin to Gr. pravana sloping, inclined, and also to L. pro forward, for. See Pro-.

prong.etymology: Cf. D. prangen to pinch, press, LG. prange a stick, or W. procio to thrust, E. prowl, pang.

pronominal.etymology: L. pronominalis: cf. F. pronominal. See Pronoun.

pronoun.etymology: Pref. pro- + noun: cf. F. pronom, L. pronomen. See Noun.

pronounce.etymology: F. prononcer, L. pronunciare; pro before, forth + nunciare, nuntiare, to announce. See Announce.

pronunciation.etymology: From Middle English pronunciacioun , from Middle French prononciation , pronunciation , from Latin prōnūntiātiō , noun of action from perfect passive participle prōnūntiātus , from verb prōnūntiāre ( “ proclaim ” ) , from prō- ( “ for ” ) + nūntiāre ( “ announce ” ) . Doublet of pronuntiatio .

proof.etymology: OF. prove, proeve, F. preuve, fr. L. proba, fr. probare to prove. See Prove.

prop.etymology: Akin to LG. & D. proppen to cram, stuff, thrust into, stop, G. pfropfen, Dan. proppe, Sw. proppa; of uncertain origin, cf. G. pfropfen to graft, fr. L. propago set, layer of a plant, slip, shoot. Cf. 3d. Prop, Propagate.

propaganda.etymology: Abbrev. fr. L. de propaganda fide: cf. F. propagande. See Propagate.

propagate.etymology: L. propagatus, p. p. of propagare to propagate, akin to propages, propago, a layer of a plant, slip, shoot. See Pro-, and cf. Pact, Prop, Prune, v. t.

propel.etymology: L. propellere, propulsum; pro forward + pellere to drive. See Pulse a beating.

proper.etymology: OE. propre, F. propre, fr. L. proprius. Cf. Appropriate.

property.etymology: OE. proprete, OF. propreté property, F. propreté neatness, cleanliness, propriété property, fr. L. proprietas. See Proper, a., and cf. Propriety.

prophecy.etymology: OE. prophecie, OF. profecie, F. prophétie, L. prophetia, fr. Gr. , fr. Prophet.

prophet.etymology: F. prophète, L. propheta, fr. Gr. Fame.

propinquity.etymology: L. propinquitas, from propinquus near, neighboring, from prope near.

propitiate.etymology: L. propitiatus, p. p. of propitiare to propitiate, fr. propitius favorable. See Propitious.

propitious.etymology: L. propitius, perhaps originally a term of augury meaning, flying forward (pro) or well; cf. Skr. pat to fly, E. petition, feather.

proportion.etymology: F., fr. L. proportio; pro before + portio part or share. See Portion.

propose.etymology: F. proposer; pref. pro- (L. pro for, forward) + poser to place. See Pose, v.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of, in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, to go before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, part spoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to look out for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a person acting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according to parts.

proposition.etymology: L. propositio: cf. F. proposition. See Propound.

propound.etymology: From earlier propone, L. proponere, propositum, to set forth, propose, propound; pro for, before + ponere to put. See Position, and cf. Provost.

proprietary.etymology: L. proprietarius: cf. F. propriétaire. See Propriety, and cf. Proprietor.

proprietor.etymology: For older proprietary: cf. F. propriétarie.

propriety.etymology: F. propriété, L. proprietas, fr. proprius one's own, proper. See Property, Proper.

roots.meaning: A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.

prorate.etymology: From L. pro rata (sc. parte) according to a certain part, in proportion.

prorogue.etymology: F. proroger, L. prorogare, prorogatum; pro forward + rogare to ask, to ask one for his opinion or vote, or about a law. See Rogation.

prosaic.etymology: L. prosaius, from prosa prose: cf. F,. prosaïque. See Prose.

proscribe.etymology: L. proscribere, proscriptum, to write before, to publish, proscribe; pro before + scribere to write. See Scribe. The sense of this word originated in the Roman practice of writing the names of persons doomed to death, and posting the list in public.

prose.etymology: F. prose, L. prosa, fr. prorsus, prosus, straight forward, straight on, for proversus; pro forward + versus, p. p. of vertere to turn. See Verse.

prosecute.etymology: L. prosecutus, p. p. of prosequi to follow, pursue. See Pursue.

prosody.etymology: L. prosodia the tone or accent of a syllable, Gr. prosodie. See Ode.

prospect.etymology: L. prospectus, fr. prospicere, prospectum, to look forward; pro before, forward + specere, spicere, look, to see: cf. OF. prospect. See Spy, v., and cf. Prospectus.

prospective.etymology: L. prospectivus: cf. F. prospectif. See Prospect, n.

prospectus.etymology: L., a prospect, sight, view: cf. F. prospectus. See Prospect.

prosper.etymology: F. prospérer v. i., or L. prosperare, v. i., or L. prosperare, v. t., fr. prosper or prosperus. See Prosperous.

prosperity.etymology: F. prospérité, L. prosperitas. See Prosperous.

prosperous.etymology: L. prosperus or prosper, originally, answering to hope; pro according to + the root of sperare to hope. See Despair.

prospicience.etymology: L. prospicientia, fr. prospiciens, p. pr. of prospicere. See Prospect.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

prostitute.etymology: L. prostitutus, p. p. of prostituere to prostitute; pro before, forth + statuere to put, place. See Statute.

prostrate.etymology: L. prostratus, p. p. of prosternere to prostrate; pro before, forward + sternere to spread out, throw down. See Stratum.

protect.etymology: L. protectus, p. p. of protegere, literally, to cover in front; pro before + tegere to cover. See Tegument.

protege.etymology: F., p. p. of protéger. See Protect.

protegee.etymology: F., p. p. of protéger. See Protect.

protein.etymology: Gr. prw os first: cf. prwtei^on the first place.

protest.etymology: F. protester, L. protestari, pro before + testari to be a witness, testis a witness. See Testify.

protestant.etymology: F. protestant, fr. L. protestans, -antis, p. pr. of protestare. See Protest, v.

protestation.etymology: L. protestatio: cf. F. protestation. See Protest.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of, in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, to go before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, part spoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to look out for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a person acting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according to parts.

prototype.etymology: F., from L. prototypus original, primitive, Gr. Proto-, and Type

protract.etymology: L. protractus, p. p. of protrahere to forth, protract; pro forward + trahere to draw. See Portrait, Portray.

protrude.etymology: L. protrudere, protrusum; pro forward + trudere to thrust. See Threat.

protuberant.etymology: L. protuberans, -antis, p. pr. of protuberare. See Protuberate.

protuberate.etymology: L. protuberare; pro forward + tuber a hump, protuberance. See Tuber.

proud.etymology: OE. proud, prout, prud, prut, AS. prut; akin to Icel. pruedhr stately, handsome, Dan. prud handsome. Cf. Pride.

prove.etymology: OE. prover, F. prouver, fr. L. probare to try, approve, prove, fr. probus good, proper. Cf. Probable, Proof, Probe.

provenance.etymology: F., fr. provenir to originate, to come forth, L. provenire. Cf. Provenience.

provencal.etymology: F., fr. Provence, fr. L. provincia province. See Provincial.

provender.etymology: OE. provende, F. provende, provisions, provender, fr. LL. praebenda (prae and pro being confused), a daily allowance of provisions, a prebend. See Prebend.

provenience.etymology: L. proveniens, -entis, p.pr. of provenire to come forth; pro forth + venire to come.

proverb.etymology: OE. proverbe, F. proverbe, from L. proverbium; pro before, for + verbum a word. See Verb.

provide.etymology: L. providere, provisum; pro before + videre to see. See Vision, and cf. Prudent, Purvey.

providence.etymology: L. providentia: cf. F. providence. See Provident, and cf. Prudence.

provident.etymology: L. providens, -entis, p. pr. of providere: cf. F. provident. See Provide, and cf. Prudent.

province.etymology: F., fr. L. provincia; prob. fr. pro before, for + the root of vincere to conquer. See Victor.

provincial.etymology: L. provincialis: cf. F. provincial. See Province, and cf. Provencal.

provision.etymology: L. provisio: cf. F. provision. See Provide.

proviso.etymology: L., (it) being provided, abl. of provisus, p. p. of providere. See Provide, and cf. Purview.

provocation.etymology: F. provocation, L. provocatio. See Provoke.

provoke.etymology: F. provoquer, L. provocare to call forth; pro forth + vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice, cry, call. See Voice.

provost.etymology: OF. provost (L. prae and pro being confused), F. prevôt, fr. L. praepositus placed before, a chief, fr. praeponere to place before: cf. AS. prafost, profast. See Preposition, and cf. Propound.

prow.etymology: F. proue (cf. Sp. & Pg. proa, It. prua), L. prora, Gr. Pro-, and cf. Prore.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of, in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, to go before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, part spoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to look out for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a person acting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according to parts.

prowess.etymology: OF. proece, proesce, F. prouesse. See Prow, a.

prowl.etymology: OE. prollen to search about; of uncertain origin, perh. for proglen, a dim. of prog to beg, or proke to poke. Cf. Proke.

proximate.etymology: L. proximatus, p. p. of proximare to come near, to approach, fr. proximus the nearest, nest, superl. of propior nearer, and prope, adv., near.

proximity.etymology: L. proximitas: cf. F. proximité See Proximate, and cf. Propinquity, Approach.

proximo.etymology: L., on the next, abl. of proximus next.

prude.etymology: F., prudish, originally, discreet, modest; shortened from OF. prudefeme, preudefeme, a discreet or excellent woman; OF. preu, prou, excellent, brave + de of + fete woman. See Prow, a., Prowess.

prudence.etymology: F., fr. L. prudentia, contr. from providentia. See Prudent, and cf. Providence.

prudent.etymology: L. prudens, -entis, contr. from providens: cf. F. prudent. See Provident.

prune.etymology: OE. proine, probably fr. F. provigner to lay down vine stocks for propagation; hence, probably, the meaning, to cut away superfluous shoots. See Provine.

prunella.etymology: NL., perhaps from G. bræune quinsy, croup.

prurient.etymology: L. pruries, -entis, p. pr. of prurire to itch. Cf. Freeze.

prurigo.etymology: L., an itching, the itch, fr. prurire to itch.

prussian.etymology: From Prussia, the country: cf. F. prussien.

pry.etymology: Corrupted fr. prize a lever. See Prize, n.

psalm.etymology: OE. psalm, salm, AS. sealm, L. psalmus, psalma, fr. Gr. psalme, salme, F. psaume.

psalmist.etymology: L. psalmista, Gr. psalmiste. See Psalm.

psalmody.etymology: Gr. psalmodie, LL. psalmodia. See Psalm, and Ode.

psalter.etymology: OE. psauter, sauter, OF. sautier, psaltier, F. psautier, from L. psalterium. See Psaltery.

psaltery.etymology: OE. sautrie, OF. psalterie, F. psaltérion, L. psalterium psaltery, psalter, from Gr. Psalm, Psalter.

pseudonymous.etymology: Gr. pseudonyme. See Pseudo-, and Name.

psychology.etymology: From French psychologie , from Renaissance Latin psychologia , from Ancient Greek ψυχή ( psukhḗ , “ soul ” ) + -λογία ( -logía , “ study of ” ) , equivalent to psycho- +‎ -logy . The Latin term is believed by some to have been coined in a lost treatise by Croatian humanist Marko Marulić (1450–1524), but this is disputed by other scholars. It is first attested in the 1570s, at which time it was apparently already current, and may be a Hellenization of the established expression dē animā ( “ on the soul ” ) in titles.

psychrometer.etymology: Gr. psychro`s cold + -meter: cf. F. psychromètre.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

ptarmigan.etymology: Gael. tarmachan; cf. Ir. tarmochan, tarmonach.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

puberty.etymology: L. pubertas, fr. puber, pubes, adult: cf. F. puberté.

pubes.etymology: L., the hair which appears on the body at puberty, from pubes adult.

pubescent.etymology: L. pubescens, -entis, p. pr. of pubescere to reach puberty, to grow hairy or mossy, fr. pubes pubes: cf. F. pubescent.

public.etymology: L. publicus, poblicus, fr. populus people: cf. F. public. See People.

publican.etymology: L. publicanus: cf. F. publicain. See Public.

publication.etymology: L. publicatio confiscation: cf. F. publication. See Publish.

publish.etymology: F. publier, L. publicare, publicatum. See Public, and -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

puce.etymology: F., fr. puce a flea, L. pulex, pulicis.

puck.etymology: OE. pouke; cf. OSw. puke, Icel. puki an evil demon, W. pwca a hobgoblin. Cf. Poker a bugbear, Pug.

pucker.etymology: From Poke a pocket, small bag.

pudding.etymology: Cf. F. boudin black pudding, sausage, L. botulus, botellus, a sausage, G. & Sw. pudding pudding, Dan. podding, pudding, LG. puddig thick, stumpy, W. poten, potten, also E. pod, pout, v.

puddle.etymology: OE. podel; cf. LG. pudel, Ir. & Gael. plod pool.

pueblo.etymology: Sp., a village, L. populus people. See People.

puerile.etymology: L. puerilis, fr. puer a child, a boy: cf. F. puéril.

puerperal.etymology: L. puerpera a lying-in woman; puer child + parere to bear: cf. F. puerpéral.

puff.etymology: Akin to G. & Sw. puff a blow, Dan. puf, D. pof; of imitative origin. Cf. Buffet.

pug.etymology: Cf. G. pucken to thump. beat.

pugilism.etymology: L. pugil a pugilist, boxer, akin to pugnus the fist. Cf. Pugnacious, Fist.

pugnacious.etymology: L. pugnax, -acis, fr. pugnare to fight. Cf. Pugilism, Fist.

puissance.etymology: F., fr.puissant. See Puissant, and cf. Potency, Potance, Potence.

puissant.etymology: F., originally, a p. pr. formed fr. L. posse to be able: cf. L. potens powerful. See Potent.

puke.etymology: Cf. G. spucken to spit, and E. spew.

pule.etymology: F. piauler; cf. L. pipilare, pipire, to peep, pip, chirp, and E. peep to chirp.

pull.etymology: AS. pullian; cf. LG. pulen, and Gael. peall, piol, spiol.

pullet.etymology: OE. polete, OF. polete, F. poulette, dim. of poule a hen, fr. L. pullus a young animal, a young fowl. See Foal, and cf. Poult, Poultry, Pool stake.

pulley.etymology: F. poulie, perhaps of Teutonic origin (cf. Poll, b. t.); but cf. OE. poleine, polive, pulley, LL. polanus, and F. poulain, properly, a colt, fr. L. pullus young animal, foal (cf. Pullet, Foal). For the change of sense, cf. F. poutre beam, originally, a filly, and E. easel.

pullulate.etymology: L. pullulatus, p. p. of pullulare to sprout, from pullulus a young animal, a sprout, dim. of pullus. See pullet.

pulmonary.etymology: L. pulmonarius, from pulmo, -onis, a lung; of uncertain origin, perh. named from its lightness, and akin to E. float: cf. F. pulmonaire. Cf. Pneumonia.

pulmonata.etymology: NL., from L. pulmo, -onis, a lung.

pulmonic.etymology: L. pulmo, -onis, a lung: cf. F. pulmonique.

pulp.etymology: L. pulpa flesh, pith, pulp of fruit: cf. F. pulpe.

pulpit.etymology: L. pulpitum: cf. OF. pulpite, F. pulpitre.

pulsate.etymology: L. pulsatus, p. p. of pulsare to beat, strike, v. intens. fr. pellere to beat, strike, drive. See Pulse a beating, and cf. Pulse, v.

pulsation.etymology: L. pulsatio a beating or striking: cf. F. pulsation.

pulse.etymology: OE. puls, L. puls, pultis, a thick pap or pottage made of meal, pulse, etc. See Poultice, and cf. Pousse.

pulverize.etymology: F. pulvériser, L. pulverizare, fr. pulvis dust, powder. See Powder.

pumice.etymology: L. pumex, pumicis, prob. akin to spuma foam: cf. AS. pumic-stan. Cf. Pounce a powder, Spume.

pump.etymology: Probably so called as being worn for pomp or ornament. See Pomp.

pumpkin.etymology: For older pompion, pompon, OF. pompon, L. pepo, peponis, Gr. Cook, n.

punch.etymology: Hind. panch five, Skr. pacan. So called because composed of five ingredients, viz., sugar, arrack, spice, water, and lemon juice. See Five.

punctilio.etymology: It. puntiglio, or Sp. puntillo, dim. fr. L. punctum point. See Point, n.

punctual.etymology: F. ponctuel (cf. Sp.puntual, It. puntuale), from L. punctum point. See Point.

puncture.etymology: L. punctura, fr. pungere, punctum, to prick. See Pungent.

pundit.etymology: Hind. pandit, Skr. pandita a learned man.

pungent.etymology: L. pungens, -entis, p. pr. of pungere, punctum, to prick. Cf. Compunction, Expunge, Poignant, Point, n., Puncheon, Punctilio, Punt, v. t.

punic.etymology: L. Punicus pertaining to Carthage, or its inhabitants, fr. Poeni the Carthaginians.

punish.etymology: OE. punischen, F. punir, from L. punire, punitum, akin to poena punishment, penalty. See Pain, and -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

punnet.etymology: Cf. Ir. buinne a shoot, branch.

punt.etymology: F. ponter, or It. puntare, fr. L. punctum point. See Point.

punter.etymology: Cf. F. ponte. See Punt, v. t.

puny.etymology: F. puîté younger, later born, OF. puisné; puis afterwards (L. post; see Post-) + né born, L. natus. See Natal, and cf. Puisne.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying behind, back, after; as, postcommissure, postdot, postscript.

pupa.etymology: L. pupa girl. doll, puppet, fem. of pupus. Cf. Puppet.

pupil.etymology: F. pupille, n. fem., L. pupilla the pupil of the eye, originally dim. of pupa a girl. See Puppet, and cf. Pupil a scholar.

pupillary.etymology: L. pupillaris: cf. F.pupillaire. See Pupil.

puppet.etymology: OE. popet, OF. poupette; akin to F. poupée a doll, probably from L. puppa, pupa, a girl, doll, puppet. Cf. Poupeton, Pupa, Pupil, Puppy.

puppy.etymology: F. poupée doll, puppet. See Puppet, and cf. Pup, n.

purana.etymology: Skr. pura, properly. old, ancient, fr. pura formerly.

purblind.etymology: For pure-blind, i. e., wholly blind. See Pure, and cf. Poreblind.

purchase.etymology: OE. purchasen, porchacen, OF. porchacier, purchacier, to pursue, to seek eagerly, F. pourchasser; OF. pour, por, pur, for (L. pro) + chacier to pursue, to chase. See Chase.

pure.etymology: OE. pur, F. pur, fr. L. purus; akin to putus pure, clear, putare to clean, trim, prune, set in order, settle, reckon, consider, think, Skr. p to clean, and perh. E. fire. Cf. Putative.

purgation.etymology: L. purgatio: cf. F. purgation. See Purge.

purge.etymology: F. purger, L. purgare; purus pure + agere to make, to do. See Pure, and Agent.

purification.etymology: F. purification, L. purificatio. See Purify.

purify.etymology: F.purifier, L. purificare; purus pure + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Pure, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

purim.etymology: Heb. pur, pl. purim, a lot.

purity.etymology: OE. purete, purte, OF. purté, F. pureté, from L. puritas, fr. purus pure. See Pure.

purl.etymology: Contr. fr. purfile, purfle. See Purfle.

purlieu.etymology: Corrupted (by influence of lieu place) fr. OF. puralée, poralée (equiv. to LL. perambulatio a survey of boundaries, originally, a going through); por (L. pro, confused, however, with L. per through) + alée. See Pro-, and Alley.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying before, in front, forth, for, in behalf of, in place of, according to; as, propose, to place before; proceed, to go before or forward; project, to throw forward; prologue, part spoken before (the main piece); propel, prognathous; provide, to look out for; pronoun, a word instead of a noun; proconsul, a person acting in place of a consul; proportion, arrangement according to parts.

purloin.etymology: OF. purloignier, porloignier, to retard, delay; pur, por, pour, for (L. pro) + loin far, far off (L. longe). See Prolong, and cf. Eloign.

purple.etymology: OE. purpre, pourpre, OF. purpre, porpre, pourpre, F. pourpre, L. purpura purple fish, purple dye, fr. Gr. furere to rage, E. fury: cf. AS. purpure. Cf. Porphyry, Purpure.

purport.etymology: OF. purport; pur, pour, for (L. pro) + porter to bear, carry. See Port demeanor.

purpose.etymology: OF. purpos, pourpos, propos, L. propositum. See Propound.

purpura.etymology: L., purple, purple fish: cf. F. purpura. See Purple.

purse.etymology: OE. purs, pors, OF. burse, borse, bourse, F. bourse, LL. bursa, fr. Gr. Bourse, Bursch, Bursar, Buskin.

purslane.etymology: OF. porcelaine, pourcelaine (cf. It. porcellana), corrupted fr. L. porcilaca for portulaca.

pursuant.etymology: From Pursue: cf. OE. poursuiant. Cf. Pursuivant.

pursue.etymology: OE. pursuen, porsuen, OF. porsivre, poursuivre, poursuir, F. poursuivre, fr. L. prosequi; pro forward + sequi to follow. See Sue, and cf. Prosecute, Pursuivant.

pursuit.etymology: F. poursuite, fr. poursuivre. See Pursue, v. t.

pursy.etymology: OF. pourcif, poulsif, poussif, fr. pousser to push, thrust, heave, OF. also poulser: cf. F. pousse the heaves, asthma. See Push.

purulent.etymology: L. purulentus, fr. pus, puris, pus, matter: cf. F. purulent. See Pus.

purvey.etymology: OE. purveien, porveien, OF. porveeir, porveoir, F. pourvoir, fr. L. providere. See Provide, and cf. Purview.

purveyor.etymology: OE. porveour, OF. pourveor, F. pourvoyeur. See Purvey, and cf. Proveditor.

purview.etymology: OF. purveu, pourveu, F. pourvu, provided, p. p. of OF. porveoir, F. pourvoir. See Purvey, View, and cf. Proviso.

pus.etymology: L., akin to Gr. foul: cf. F. pus. See Foul, a.

pusillanimous.etymology: L. pusillannimis; pusillus very little (dim. of pusus a little boy; cf. puer a boy, E. puerile) + animus the mind: cf. F. pusillanime. See Animosity.

puss.etymology: Cf. D. poes, Ir. & Gael. pus.

pustulate.etymology: L. pustulatus, p. p. of pustulare to blister, fr. pustula. See Pustule.

pustule.etymology: L. pustula, and pusula: cf. F. pustule.

putative.etymology: L. putativus, fr. putare, putatum, to reckon, suppose, adjust, prune, cleanse. See Pure, and cf. Amputate, Compute, Dispute, Impute.

putrefaction.etymology: L. putrefactio: cf. F. putréfaction. See Putrefy.

putrefy.etymology: F. putréfier; L. putrere to be rotten + -ficare (in. comp.) to make; cf. L. putrefacere. See Putrid, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

putrescent.etymology: L. putrescens, p. pr.of putrescere to grow rotten, v. incho. fr. putrere to be rotten. See Putrid.

putrid.etymology: L. putridus, fr. putrere to be rotten, fr.puter, or putris, rotten, fr. putere to stink, to be rotten: cf. F. putride. See Pus, Foul, a.

putty.etymology: F. potée, fr. pot pot; what was formerly called putty being a substance resembling what is now called putty powder, and in part made of the metal of old pots. See Pot.

puzzle.etymology: For opposal, in the sense of problem. See Oppose, Pose, v.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

pyralid.etymology: L. pyralis, -idis, a kind of winged insect.

pyrope.etymology: L. pyropus a kind of red bronze, fr. Gr. pyrope.

pyrotechnic.etymology: Pyro- + technic, technical: cf. F. pyrotechnique. See Fire, Technical.

pyrotechnical.etymology: Pyro- + technic, technical: cf. F. pyrotechnique. See Fire, Technical.

pyrus.etymology: L. pyrus, or better pirus, pear tree.

pythoness.etymology: L. pythonissa: cf. F. pythonisse. See Pythian.

pyx.etymology: L. pyxis a box, Gr. Box a receptacle.
